term_table.greek_sentence: χρὴ δὲ μηδὲ κατάῤῥοπον ἐσχηματίσθαι τὸ τοιοῦτον μόριον, ἢ κεκινῆσθαι προσφάτως ὑπὲρ τὰ ἄλλα· διὸ καί τινι λόγῳ περιλαβὼν ἄν τις ἅπαντας τοὺς κατὰ μέρος διορισμοὺς, τότ’ ἐνδείκνυσθαι φήσει τὸν ὄγκον τῶν φλεβῶν αἵματος πλῆθος, ὅταν ἅπαντα τὰ μόρια τὴν αὐτὴν κατάστασιν ἔχῃ μετὰ συμμέτρου θερμασίας, ὡς εἴγε ὡσαύτως μὲν ἅπαντα διακέοιτο, θερμότης δὲ ἄμετρος ὑπάρχοι, χύσις ἐν τῷδε γίγνεται τῶν χυμῶν εἰς ὄγκον αἴρουσα τὰς φλέβας, οὐ μὴν αἱματικόν γε τὸ πλῆθος, ἀλλὰ πνευματικὸν ἐνδείκνυται· πνευματοῦνται γὰρ οἱ χυμοὶ θερμαινόμενοι, διὸ καὶ ὅσοι τὸν ὄγκον τῶν φλεβῶν ἀπεφήναντο πλῆθος σημαίνειν, ἐὰν δὴ προσυπακούσῃ τις ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τὸ κατ’ ἐκείνας τὰς φλέβας, ἐν αἷσπερ ἂν ᾖ τοῦτο γινόμενον, ὀρθῶς εἰρηκέναι δόξουσι· πλείων γὰρ ἡ οὐσία τῆς πρόσθεν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἐστὶν ἡ τὸν ὄγκον ἐργασαμένη ταῖς φλεψὶν, οὐ μὴν ἤδη γέ πω δῆλον, ὁποῖόν τι τὸ πλῆθός ﻿ [568] ἐστιν· ἁπάσης γὰρ οὐσίας πολλῆς ὁ παρὰ φύσιν ὄγκος κοινὸς, εἴτ’ οὖν αἷμα καθαρὸν, εἴτε χολῶδες, εἴτε ὀῤῥῶδες, εἴτε φλεγματικὸν, εἴτε πνευματικὸν ὑπάρχοι.

term_table.greek_sentence: ὥστε ὁ ὄγκος καὶ ἡ τονώδης αἴσθησις οὐ μᾶλλόν τι χυμῶν ἢ πνεύματος ἐνδείξεται πλῆθος.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And just as this is common to every variety of plethora, so too is the stretching of the veins; for this too follows upon the quantity of the plethora, not upon the difference in kind.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For swelling contrary to nature is common to every abundant substance, whether it be pure blood, or bilious, or serous, or phlegmatic, or pneumatic. And just as this is common to every variety of plethora, so too is the stretching of the veins; for this too follows upon the quantity of the plethora, not upon its difference in kind.

term_table.greek_sentence: χρὴ γὰρ δήπου τοῖς μεγίστοις ὄγκοις ἐζεῦχθαι τὴν τοῦ τείνεσθαι διάθεσιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: How then is it that sometimes no swelling at all appears in the veins, while the tensive sensation is strong?
term_table.english_sentence_B: How, then, is it that sometimes no swelling at all appears in the veins at the outset, and yet the tensive sensation is strong?

term_table.greek_sentence: ἢ διότι ἔστιν ὅτε ὁ ὄγκος ἐν ταῖς διὰ βάθους φλεψὶ μόναις διατείνει, ἢ εἴπερ ἐν τῷ πρὸς τὶ τὸ πλῆθος, ὑπὲρ οὗ νῦν δια λεγόμεθα, τό τε πρὸς τὴν εὐρύτητα τῶν ἀγγείων, ὃ δὴ πλῆθος λέγομεν, οὐδέπω τεινομένων αὐτῶν, τό τε πρὸς τὴν τοῦ χιτῶνος τάσιν, δηλονότι τοῦ μὲν ὄγκου τῶν φλεβῶν ἡ γένεσις ἐπιδίδοται, εἰς πλῆθος αὐξομένου τοῦ αἵματος ὑπὲρ τὴν φυσικὴν ἑκάστου συμμετρίαν, ὥστε πρὸς ἐκείνην λέγεσθαι τὸ πολύ· τὸ δὲ τείνεσθαι τὸν χιτῶνα τῆς ὡς πρὸς αὐτὸν συμμετρίας ἐνδείκνυται (διὰ) ὑπερβολήν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For surely the condition of being stretched ought to be yoked to the greatest swellings. Either it is because there are times when the swelling distends only the veins in the depth, or, if indeed the plethora about which we are now discoursing belongs among things relative to something—both that relative to the width of the vessels, which we in fact call plethora, when they are not yet being stretched, and that relative to the tension of the coat—then clearly the genesis of the swelling of the veins advances as the blood increases into plethora beyond the natural due proportion of each, so that 'much' is said relative to that; whereas the coat's being stretched indicates (διὰ) an excess over the due proportion relative to the coat itself.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For surely the condition of being stretched ought to be yoked to the very great swellings. Either it is because the swelling sometimes distends only the veins that lie in the depth; or else, if within plethora taken in relation to something, about which we are now discoursing, there is both the plethora in relation to the width of the vessels, which we call plethora, while they are not yet stretched, and the plethora in relation to the stretching of the coat, then clearly the generation of the swelling of the veins advances (ἐπιδίδοται) as the blood increases to a plethora beyond the natural due proportion of each, so that 'much' is said in relation to that proportion; whereas the stretching of the coat indicates an excess beyond the due proportion relative to the coat itself.

Vict. 2.65 ; ὑ. δισσὴ . . , τῷ ποσῷ καὶ τῷ ποιῷ Arist. Med. 232 ; ἐπέφερον τὴν ὑ. τοῦ καινοῦσθαι pushed on their extravagance in revolutionizing, Th. 3.82 ; οὐκ ἔχον ἐστὶν ὑπερβολήν it can go no further, D. 21.119 , cf. 25.54 ; ἃ μηδὲ πιθανὰς τὰς ὑ. ἔχει Men. Her. 62 ; so οὐδεμίαν or μηδεμίαν ὑ. λείπειν, Isoc. 4.5 , 110 , cf. D. 3.25 ; οὐδεμίαν ὑ. καταλείπων φιλοτιμίας SIG 545.13 (Delph., iii B. C.); εἴ τις ὑ. τούτου if there is aught beyond (worse than) this, D. 19.66 , cf. Isoc. 5.42 ; ταῦτ' οὐχ ὑ.; is not this the extreme, the last degree? D. 27.38 ; ὑπερβολὴν ποιήσομαι I will put an extreme case, Id. 19.332 ; τοσαύτην ὑ. ποιεῖσθαι ὥστε . . to go so far that . . , Id. 18.190 : folld. by a gen., ὑ. ποιεῖσθαι ἐκείνων τῆς αὑτοῦ βδελυρίας to carry his own rascality beyond theirs, Id. 22.52 , cf. 23.201 , And. 4.22 , Lys. 14.38 ; ὑ. ποιεῖν τῆς τιμῆς to raise the price, Arist. Pol. 1259a26 ; εἰς ὑ. εὐδαιμονίας ἥκειν Isoc. 11.14 ; τοσαύτας ὑ. δωρειῶν παρές χηται D. 20.141 ; ὑ. ἀνοίας ἔχειν Polystr. p.27 W. with Prep. in Adverbial phrases, = ὑπερβαλλόντως, εἰς ὑπερβολήν in excess, exceedingly; εἰς ὑ. ἄμεινον E. Fr. 494 ; ἀγαθὸς εἰς ὑ. Antiph. 80.11 ; ἐς ὑ. ἐκθερμαίνεσθαι Hp. Vict. 2.65 : c. gen., κτήσαιτ' ἂν ὄλβον εἰς ὑ. πατρός E. Fr. 282.6 ( v.l. εἰς ὑπεκτροφὴν πάτρας ); far beyond, τοῦ πρόσθεν εἰς ὑ. πανοῦργος, i. e. far more wicked, Id. Hipp. 939 , cf. D. 61.33 ; ἀναλίσκειν πάντα εἰς ὑπερβολάς Pl. Ep. 326d :— ἐξ ὑπερβολῆς Plb. 8.15.8 :—καθ' ὑπερβολὰν τοξεύσας with surpassing aim, S. OT 1196 (lyr.); καθ' ὑ. ἐπαινεῖν extravagantly, Isoc. 5.11 ; οἱ καθ' ὑ. ἐν ἐνδείᾳ ὄντες in extremity of need, Arist. Pol. 1295b18 ; αἱ καθ' ὑ. ἡδοναί Id. EN 1151a12 ; τὸ καθ' ὑ. τραχύ Phld. Rh. 1367b1 , Pol. 1284a4 ; ἡ ὑ. τῆς φιλίας the best and noblest kind of friendship, Id. EN 1166b1 ; but ἡ καθ' ὑ. φιλία, = ἡ καθ' ὑπεροχήν , Id. term_table.english_sentence_A: For surely the condition of being stretched ought to be yoked to the greatest swellings. Either it is because there are times when the swelling distends only the veins in the depth, or, if indeed the plethora about which we are now discoursing belongs among things relative to something—both that relative to the width of the vessels, which we in fact call plethora, when they are not yet being stretched, and that relative to the tension of the coat—then clearly the genesis of the swelling of the veins advances as the blood increases into plethora beyond the natural due proportion of each, so that 'much' is said relative to that; whereas the coat's being stretched indicates (διὰ) an excess over the due proportion relative to the coat itself.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For surely the condition of being stretched ought to be yoked to the very great swellings. Either it is because the swelling sometimes distends only the veins that lie in the depth; or else, if within plethora taken in relation to something, about which we are now discoursing, there is both the plethora in relation to the width of the vessels, which we call plethora, while they are not yet stretched, and the plethora in relation to the stretching of the coat, then clearly the generation of the swelling of the veins advances (ἐπιδίδοται) as the blood increases to a plethora beyond the natural due proportion of each, so that 'much' is said in relation to that proportion; whereas the stretching of the coat indicates an excess beyond the due proportion relative to the coat itself.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀμετρ-ία, ἡ, excess, disproportion, opp. συμμετρία, Pl. Ti. 87d , cf. R. 486d , Heraclit. All. 8 , Alex.Aphr. Pr. 1.112 , etc. want of moderation, Arist. VV 1251b15 . infinity, countless number, κακῶν Pl. Ax. 367a (in pl.).
term_table.greek_sentence: ἐν μὲν γὰρ τῷ φάναι· κατ’ ἀρχὰς μὲν οὖν καὶ μετρίως πληρουμένων τῶν ἀγγείων, εὐτονώτεροί τε καὶ ἰσχυρότεροι ἑαυτῶν φαίνονται παρὰ τὸ εἰθισμένον· ἐνεδείξατο τὴν ὑπὲρ τὸ κατὰ φύσιν ἑκάστῳ τοῦ αἵματος ἀμετρίαν· ἐν οἷς δὲ ἑξῆς ἐπιφέρων φησίν· ἐπιπλέον δὲ πληρώσεως ἐρχομένων, παρεμπίμπλανται βραχίονές τε καὶ χεῖρες καὶ κνῆμαι· τὴν ὡς πρὸς τοὺς περιέχοντας τὸ αἷμα χιτῶνας· ὥστε ὅρους εἶναι δύο τῆς τοῦ αἵματος ὑπὲρ τὸ κατὰ φύσιν αὐξήσεως, ἕνα μὲν ἐν τῷ πληροῦσθαι τῶν φλεβῶν τοὺς χιτῶνας εἰς ὄγκον αἰρομένους ὑπὲρ τὸ κατὰ φύσιν ἑκάστω, τὸν δὲ ἕτερον, ἐν ᾧ πρὸς τούτῳ τείνεσθαι συμβαίνει, μηδ’ ἑτέρου τούτων ὁρωμένου ἐν τῷ πρὸς τὴν δύναμιν πλήθει.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For in saying, "At the beginning, then, and when the vessels are moderately filled, they appear more well-toned and stronger than their usual selves, beyond what is customary," he indicated the disproportion of the blood beyond what is according to nature for each individual; but in what he adds next, saying, "but when they come to a greater degree of filling, the upper arms and hands and shins become filled out," he indicated that disproportion which is relative to the coats that contain the blood; so that there are two limits of the increase of the blood beyond what is according to nature: one consisting in the coats of the veins being filled, raised into a swelling beyond what is according to nature for each individual; the other, in which, in addition to this, it comes about that they are stretched—neither of these being seen in the plethora relative to the faculty.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For in saying: 'At the beginning, then, when the vessels are filled moderately, they appear more vigorous and stronger than themselves, beyond what is customary', he indicated the disproportion of the blood in excess of what is natural for each person; and in what he adds next, saying: 'but when they come further into filling, the arms and hands and shins are filled up as well', he indicated the disproportion relative to the coats that contain the blood. So there are two limits of the increase of the blood beyond what is natural: one in which the coats of the veins are filled, rising into a swelling beyond what is natural for each, and the other in which, in addition to this, it happens that they are stretched; neither of these is seen in the plethora relative to the strength.

term_table.greek_sentence: δεήσεται δὲ καὶ αὐτὸ τῶν διορισμῶν, ὧνπερ ὁ ὄγκος· [571] εἰ γὰρ διά τι τῶν ἔξωθεν, οἷον ἥλιον, ἢ λουτρὸν, ἢ γυμνάσιον, ἢ πορείαν, ἢ ἁπλῶς εἰπεῖν θερμασίαν, οὕτω δὲ καὶ θυμὸν, αἰδώ τε καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα, καὶ ὀξεῖς δὲ πυρετοὶ τούτου τοῦ γένους εἰσίν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And it too will require the same distinctions as the swelling does; [571] for if it is due to some external cause, such as sun, or a bath, or exercise, or a walk, or, to put it simply, heat—and likewise also anger, shame and all such things; and acute fevers too are of this class.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But this too will require the same qualifying distinctions as the swelling does. [571] For if it is owing to one of the external causes, such as sun, or a bath, or exercise, or walking, or, to put it simply, heating, and likewise anger, shame and all such things, then acute fevers too belong to this class.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔρευθ-ος, εος, τό, redness, flush, Hp. Epid. 1.26 . έ, Plu. 2.48c ; of dye, A.R. 1.726 ; [ἡδονὴ] ἔρευθος εἰργασμένη with painted cheeks, Ph. 2.266 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ὅταν οὖν ὁμαλὴ μὲν ὅλου τοῦ σώματος ἡ διάθεσις εἴη, μηδὲν δὲ ὧν εἴρηκα παρῇ, τότ’ ἂν εἴη τὸ ἔρευθος αἱματικοῦ πλήθους γνώρισμα τοῦ καθ’ ὅλον τὸ ζῶον· εἰ δὲ μὴ, ἀλλά γε κατ’ ἐκεῖνο τὸ μέρος, ἐν ᾧ φαίνεται· καὶ γὰρ καὶ ταῖς φλεγμοναῖς, εἴτ’ ἐν τοῖς μυσὶν εἴτ’ ἐν τοῖς δέρμασι συνίστανται, τὸ τοιοῦτον ἕπεται χρῶμα, πληθωρικοῖς ὑπάρχουσι νοσήμασιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: So when the condition of the whole body is uniform, and none of the things I have mentioned is present, then the redness would be a sign of sanguineous fullness throughout the whole animal; but if not, then at least in that part in which it appears. For such a colour also accompanies inflammations, whether they form in the muscles or in the skins, since they are plethoric diseases.
term_table.english_sentence_B: When, therefore, the condition of the whole body is uniform, and none of the things I have mentioned is present, then the redness would be a sign of a sanguineous abundance throughout the whole animal; if not, then at any rate of an abundance in that part in which it appears. For inflammations too, whether they arise in the muscles or in the skin, are attended by such a colour, since they are plethoric diseases.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἀλλὰ περὶ φλεγμονῶν αὐτάρκως ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέλεκται γράμματι, καθ’ ὃ περὶ τῶν παρὰ φύσιν ὄγκων ἐπεσκεπτόμεθα, δεικνύντες ἅπαντας αὐτοὺς ὑπὸ πλήθους ὑγρῶν ἄλλοτε εἰς ἄλλο μέρος κατασκηπτόντων συνίστασθαι· νυνὶ δὲ οὐ περὶ τούτων, ἀλλ’ ὡς εἴρηται πρόσθεν, ὑπὲρ ἐκείνου τοῦ πλήθους ὁ λόγος ἐστὶν, ὃ καλεῖται πληθώρα, πλεονεξίας χυμῶν ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ σώματι συνισταμένης.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But concerning inflammations enough has been said in another book, in which we investigated swellings contrary to nature, showing that all of them are formed by a fullness of humours descending now upon one part, now upon another; but now the discussion is not about these, but, as was said before, about that fullness which is called plethora, when an excess of humours forms in the whole body.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But concerning inflammations enough has been said in another treatise, in which we examined the swellings contrary to nature, showing that they all arise from an abundance of fluids settling down now upon one part, now upon another. Now, however, the discussion is not about these but, as was said before, about that abundance which is called plethora, when an excess of humours arises in the whole body.

HA 508b33 ; or flesh-like substance, ib. 519b29 : also of plants, ς. ἔχουσι τὸ φύλλον Thphr. HP 1.10.4 , al.; of timber, ib. 5.1.5 ; of wine, of a full body, Ath. 1.27c .
term_table.greek_sentence: κατὰ γοῦν τὸ σαρκῶδες γένος ἕτερος μὲν ὄγκος ὁ τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἐστιν, ἕτερος δὲ ὁ τῶν ὑγρῶν, ὥσπερ ἐρίου τινὸς ἢ σπογγιᾶς τῆς σαρκὸς ἐμπεπλησμένης ὑγρότητος περιττῆς· ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν τοιοῦτον πλῆθος ἐν ταῖς σαρξὶν ἀνάλογόν ἐστι τῷ κατὰ τὸ ἔγχυμα καλουμένῳ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀγγείων, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον πλῆθος τῷ πρὸς τὴν δύναμιν, ἢ μετὰ βάρους· μεμνημένων ἡμῶν, ὅτι μηδὲν διήνεγκεν, ἢ περὶ συνθέτου σαρκὸς, ἢ περὶ μυῶν διαλέγεσθαι, καὶ ὡς εἴ ποτε περὶ πλήθους ὁ λόγος γίγνοιτο τοῦ κατὰ τὰς σάρκας, τοὺς μῦς ἀκουστέον ἐστὶν, οὐ τὴν ἁπλῆν ἐκείνην σάρκα, τὴν ὑπό τινων ὀνομαζομένην παρέγχυμα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In the fleshy kind, at any rate, one bulk is that of the fleshes themselves, another that of the humours, the flesh being filled, like some wool or a sponge, with superfluous moisture; but such a plethos in the fleshes is analogous to that in the vessels which is called plethos in respect of the filling, while the other plethos is analogous to that in relation to the faculty, or with heaviness—we bearing in mind that it makes no difference whether one discourses about composite flesh or about muscles, and that if ever the discussion should come to be about the plethos in the fleshes, one must understand the muscles, not that simple flesh which is named by some parenchyma.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But this kind of abundance in the fleshes is analogous to what is called, in the case of the vessels, abundance with respect to the infused content (enchyma), while the other abundance is analogous to that relative to the faculty (δύναμις), or accompanied by heaviness. We must remember that it makes no difference whether one speaks of composite flesh or of muscles, and that whenever the discussion is about the abundance in the fleshes, one must understand the muscles, not that simple flesh which is named parenchyma by some.

term_table.greek_sentence: κατὰ γοῦν τὸ σαρκῶδες γένος ἕτερος μὲν ὄγκος ὁ τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἐστιν, ἕτερος δὲ ὁ τῶν ὑγρῶν, ὥσπερ ἐρίου τινὸς ἢ σπογγιᾶς τῆς σαρκὸς ἐμπεπλησμένης ὑγρότητος περιττῆς· ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν τοιοῦτον πλῆθος ἐν ταῖς σαρξὶν ἀνάλογόν ἐστι τῷ κατὰ τὸ ἔγχυμα καλουμένῳ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀγγείων, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον πλῆθος τῷ πρὸς τὴν δύναμιν, ἢ μετὰ βάρους· μεμνημένων ἡμῶν, ὅτι μηδὲν διήνεγκεν, ἢ περὶ συνθέτου σαρκὸς, ἢ περὶ μυῶν διαλέγεσθαι, καὶ ὡς εἴ ποτε περὶ πλήθους ὁ λόγος γίγνοιτο τοῦ κατὰ τὰς σάρκας, τοὺς μῦς ἀκουστέον ἐστὶν, οὐ τὴν ἁπλῆν ἐκείνην σάρκα, τὴν ὑπό τινων ὀνομαζομένην παρέγχυμα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In the fleshy kind, at any rate, one bulk is that of the fleshes themselves, another that of the humours, the flesh being filled, like some wool or a sponge, with superfluous moisture; but such a plethos in the fleshes is analogous to that in the vessels which is called plethos in respect of the filling, while the other plethos is analogous to that in relation to the faculty, or with heaviness—we bearing in mind that it makes no difference whether one discourses about composite flesh or about muscles, and that if ever the discussion should come to be about the plethos in the fleshes, one must understand the muscles, not that simple flesh which is named by some parenchyma.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But this kind of abundance in the fleshes is analogous to what is called, in the case of the vessels, abundance with respect to the infused content (enchyma), while the other abundance is analogous to that relative to the faculty (δύναμις), or accompanied by heaviness. We must remember that it makes no difference whether one speaks of composite flesh or of muscles, and that whenever the discussion is about the abundance in the fleshes, one must understand the muscles, not that simple flesh which is named parenchyma by some.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: περισσός, Att. περιττός, ή, όν, (from περί, as ἔπισσαι from ἐπί, μέτασσαι from μετά) beyond the regular number or size, prodigious, δῶρα Hes. Th. 399 (never in Hom. ); ῶʼμος Trag.Adesp. 458.3 ; στάθμα, dub.sens., v. ἕλκω B. 3 . out of the common, extraordinary, strange, ἔ τι περισσὸν εἰδείη if he has any signal knowledge, Thgn. 769 ; εἴ τι φρονεῖς καί τι περισσὸν ἔχεις Philisc.( PLG 2.327 ); π. λόγος S. OT 841 ; ἄγρα E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); πάθος Id. Supp. 791 (lyr.); βίος οὐδὲν ἔχων π. ἀλλὰ πάντα σμικρά Antipho Soph. 51 ; οὐ γὰρ π. οὐδὲν οὐδ' ἔξω λόγου πέπονθας E. Hipp. 437 ; περισσότερα παθήματα Antipho 3.4.5 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἔργων καὶ τερατώδη Isoc. 12.77 ; ἴδια καὶ π. Id. 15.145 ; π. καὶ θαυμαστά Arist. EN 1141b6 ; πρᾶξις π. Id. Pol. 1312a27 ; οὐθὲν δὴ λέγοντες π. φαίνονταί τι λέγειν Id. Metaph. 1053b3 ; τί π. ποιεῖτε; Ev.Matt. 5.47 ; περιττοτάτη φύσις Arist. HA 531a9 ; συνανθρωπίζον . . πάντων περισσότατον, of the dog, Ath. 13.611c , cf. Clearch. 24 ; in Literature, striking, τὸ περιττόν, as a quality of οἱ τοῦ Σωκράτους λόγοι, Arist. Pol. 1265a11 ; τὰ σοφὰ καὶ τὰ π. refinements, Epicur. Fr. 409 ; opp. κοινὸς καὶ δημώδης, Longin. 40.2 (but also, elaborate, π. καὶ πεποιημένος Id. 3.4 ; in bad sense, far-fetched, D.H. Pomp. 2 , Dem. 56 ). of persons, extraordinary, remarkable, esp. for great learning, π. ὢν ἀνήρ E. Hipp. 948 ; τοὺς . . π. καί τι πράσσοντας πλέον Id. Fr. 788 ; δυστυχεῖς εἶναι τοὺς π. Arist. Metaph. 983a2 ; π. γένος τῶν μελιττῶν Id. GA 760a4 : freq. with the manner added, π. κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν Id. Pr. 953a10 ; περὶ τὸν ἄλλον βίον περιττότερος somewhat extravagant or eccentric, Id. Pol. 1267 b24 ; τῇ φύσει π. Id. HA 622b6 ; κάλλει Plu. Demetr. 2 ; ἐν ἅπασι Id. Dem. 3 ; τὴν ὥραν Alciphr. 1.12 : c. inf., D.H. Comp. 18 . c. gen., περισσὸς ἄλλων πρός τι beyond others in . . , S. El. 155 ; θύσει τοῦδε περισσότερα greater things than this, AP 6.321 (Leon. Alex. ); περιττότερος προφήτου one greater than . . , Ev.Matt. 11.9 . more than sufficient, superfluous, αἱ π. δαπάναι X. Mem. 3.6.6 ; περιττὸν ἔχειν to have a surplus, Id. An. 7.6.31 ; οἱ μὲν . . περιττὰ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ οὐδὲ τὰ ἀναγκαῖα . . Id. Oec. 20.1 : c. gen., τῶν ἀρκούντων περιττά more than sufficient, Id. Cyr. 8.2.21 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἱκανῶν Id. Hier. 1.19 : freq. in military sense, οἱ π. ἱππεῖς the reserve horse, Id. Eq.Mag. 8.14 ; οἱ π. τῆς φυλακῆς ib. 7.7 ; π. σκηναί spare tents, Id. Cyr. 4.6.12 (but τοῖς περιττοῖς χρήσεσθαι their superior numbers, Id. An. 4.8.11 , cf. Cyr. 6.3.20 ); τὸ π. the surplus, residue, Inscr. ap. eund. An. 5.3.13 (but τὸ π. τοῦ Ἰουδαίου the advantage of the Jew, Ep.Rom. 3.1 ); Ἁρπυιῶν τὰ π. their leavings, AP 11.239 ( Lucill. ); τὸ π. τῆς ἡμέρας the remainder of the day, X.Eph. 1.3 ; π. γράμματα supplementary provisions in a will, BGU 326ii9 (ii A.D.). in bad sense, superfluous, useless, οὐδέ τι τοῦ παντὸς κενεὸν πέλει οὐδὲ π. Emp. 13 ; μόχθος π. A. Pr. 385 , cf. S. Ant. 780 ; π. κἀνόνητα σώματα Id. Aj. 758 ; βάρος π. γῆς ἀναστρωφώμενοι Id. Fr. 945 ; ἄχθος Id. El. 1241 (lyr.); τὰ γὰρ π. πανταχοῦ λυπήρ' ἔπη Id. Fr. 82 ; αὐδῶ σε μὴ περισσὰ κηρύσσειν A. Th. 1048 ; π. πάντες οὑν μέσῳ λόγοι E. Med. 819 ; π. φωνῶν Id. Supp. 459 . excessive, extravagant, μηχανᾶσθαι περισσά commit extravagances, Hdt. 2.32 ; περισσὰ δρᾶν, πράσσειν, to be over-busy, S. Tr. 617 , Ant. 68 ; π. φρονεῖν to be over-wise, E. Fr. 924 (anap.); ἡ π. αὕτη ἐπιμέλεια τοῦ σώματος Pl. R. 407b ; μῆκος πολὺ λόγων π. Id. Lg. 645c ; redundant, overdone, οἱ καρτεροὶ καὶ π. λόγοι Id. Ax. 365c , etc.; of dress, ἐσθὴς π. Plu. 2.615d ; περισσοτέρα λύπη 2 Ep.Cor. 2.7 ; τοῦ τὰ δέοντ' ἔχειν περιττὰ μισῶ I hate extravagance in comparison with moderation, Alex. 254 , etc. of persons, over-wise, over-curious, περισσὸς καὶ φρονῶν μέγα E. Hipp. 445 , cf. Ba. 429 (lyr.); ὁ πολυπράγμων καὶ π. Plb. 9.1.4 ; τὴν περὶ τὸ σῶμα θεραπείαν ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. Plu. Cic. 8 ; so, of speakers, π. ἐν τοῖς λόγοις Δημοσθένης Aeschin. 1.119 . as a term of praise, subtle, acute, ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. διάνοια Arist. Top. 141b13 . Arith., ἀριθμὸς π. an odd, uneven number, opp. ἄρτιος, Epich. 170.7 , Philol. 5 , Pl. Prt. 356e , etc.; π. ἡμέραι Hp. Aph. 4.61 ; τὸ π. καὶ τὸ ἄρτιον the nature of odd and even, Pl. Grg. 451c , etc.; π. χῶραι the odd places in a verse, Heph. 5.1 ; ἀρτιάκις π. ἀριθμός a number divisible by an odd number an even number of times, as 2 , 6 , 10 , Euc. 7 Def. 9 . περισσότεροι more in number, extra, Carnead. ap. S.E. M. 9.140 . περιττόν, τό, = στρύχνος μανικός, θρύον 11 , Thphr. HP 9.11.6 ; περισσόν Dsc. 4.73 ; περίσκον Orib. 12.8.56 . Adv. περισσῶς extraordinarily, exceedingly, θεοσεβέεες π. ἐόντες Hdt. 2.37 ; ἐπαινέσεται π. E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); π. παῖδας ἐκδιδάσκεσθαι to have them educated overmuch, Id. Med. 295 ; περιττοτέρως τῶν ἄλλων far above all others, Isoc. 3.44 ; περισσότερον τοῦ ἑνός Luc. Pr.Im. 14 ; also περισσά Pi. N. 7.43 , E. Hec. 579 , etc. remarkably, περισσότερον τῶν ἄλλων θάψαι τινά more sumptuously, Hdt. 2.129 ; οἴκησις π. ἐσκευασμένη Plb. 1.29.7 ; περιττότατα ἔχειν to be most remarkable, Arist. HA 589a31 ; κοσμουμένη π. καὶ σεμνῶς Plu. 2.145e ; περισσότατα ἀνθρώπων θρησκεύειν in the most singular way, D.C. 37.17 ; ἡδέως καὶ π. in an uncommon manner, D.H. Comp. 3 ; εἰπεῖν στρογγύλως καὶ π. Id. Is. 20 ; ἰδίως καὶ π. Plu. Thes. 19 ; τὰ καινῶς ἱστορούμενα καὶ π. Id. 2.30d . abundantly, ἐχέτω π. τῆς κρόκης Alciphr. 3.41 . with a neg., οὐδὲν περισσὸν τούτων nothing more than or beyond these, Antipho 3.4.6 ; οὐδὲν τῶν ἄλλων περιττότερον πραγματεύεσθαι Pl. Ap. 20c ; οὐδὲν π. ἢ εἰ . . no otherwise than if . . , Id. Smp. 219c ; περισσόν alone, furthermore, LXX Ec. 12.12 ,al. τὰ περισσά in vain, AP 12.182 ( Strat. ). ἐκ περιττοῦ superfluously, uselessly, Pl. Prt. 338c , Sph. 265e ; but ὑπερέχειν ἐκ π. to be far superior, Id. Lg. 734d , cf. 802d ; ἡ κάμινος ἐκαύθη ἐκ π. Thd. Da. 3.22 ; ἐκ π. χρησάμενος τῇ παρρησίᾳ Luc. Pro Merc.Cond. 13 ; cf. ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: σάρξ, gen. σαρκός, ἡ , Aeol. σύρξ EM 708.31 :— flesh, Hom. always in pl., exc. Od. 19.450 , cf. Hes. Sc. 364 , 461 ; κορέει κύνας . . δημῷ καὶ σάρκεσσι Il. 8.380 ; ἔγκατά τε σάρκας τε καὶ ὀστέα Od. 9.293 , cf. 11.219 ; σάρκες περιτρομέοντο μέλεσσιν 18.77 , cf. Hes. Th. 538 , Pi. Fr. 168 , etc.; τούτου σάρκας λύκοι πάσονται A. Th. 1040 ; ὀπτὰς σάρκας Id. Ag. 1097 ; σάρκες δ' ἀπ' ὀστέων . . ἀπέρρεον E. Med. 1200 ; sts. to represent the whole body, μήτε γῆ δέξαιτό μου σάρκας θανόντος Id. Hipp. 1031 , cf. 1239 , 1343 (anap.): sg. later in same sense, τοῦ αἵματος . . πηγνυμένου ς. γίνεται (of the foetus) Hp. Nat.Puer. 15 , cf. Steril. 233 ; κορέσαι στόμα πρὸς χάριν ἐμᾶς σαρκὸς αἰόλας S. Ph. 1157 (lyr.); ἔδαπτον σάρκα E. Med. 1189 , cf. Ba. 1136 , Cyc. 344 , etc.: also collectively, of the body, γέροντα τὸν νοῦν, σάρκα δ' ἡβῶσαν φέρει A. Th. 622 ; σαρκὶ παλαιᾶ Id. Ag. 72 (anap.); σαρκὸς περιβόλαια, ἐνδυτά, E. HF 1269 , Ba. 746 :— Pl. uses sg. and pl. in much the same manner, ταῖς σαρξὶ σάρκες προσγένωνται Phd. 96d , cf. Smp. 211e , R. 556d , Grg. 518c , etc.; τῆς σαρκὸς διαλυτικόν Ti. 60b , cf. 61c , 62b , etc.: portions of meat, usu. in pl., σάρκας τρεῖς IG 12(7).237.17 (Amorgos) (sg., ib. 12(2).498.16 (Methymna, iii B.C.)); but, pieces of flesh or membrane, βήσσοντα . . ὥστε σάρκας ἐνπύους . . ἀποβάλλειν SIG 1171.5 (Lebena). εἰς σάρκα πημαίνειν to the quick, Phld. Herc. 1289p.60V. ἡ ς. τοῦ σκύτεος the inner or flesh-side of leather, Hp. Art. 33 . fleshy, pulpy substance of fruit, Thphr. CP 6.8.5 , HP 1.2.6 , 4.15.1 , al. the flesh, as the seat of the affections and lusts, fleshly nature, ἐν τῇ ς. ἡ ἡδονή Epicur. Sent. 18 , cf. Sent.Vat. 33 ; ἀδούλωτον (prob. l.) τῇ σαρκὶ καὶ τοῖς ταύτης πάθεσι Plu. 2.107f , cf. 101b ; freq. in NT, Ep.Gal. 5.19 , al. in NT also, the body, τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοια Ep.Rom. 13.14 ; οὔτε ἡ ς. αὐτοῦ εἶδεν διαφθοράν Act.Ap. 2.31 , etc.: hence (partly as a Hebraism) πᾶσα σάρξ, = every-body, LXX Ge. 6.12 , al., Ev.Luc. 3.6 , etc.; οὐ . . πᾶσα σάρξ nobody, Ev. Matt. 24.22 , etc. the physical or natural order of things, opp. the spiritual or supernatural, σοφοὶ κατὰ σάρκα 1 Ep.Cor. 1.26 ; ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ καὶ οὐκ ἐν σαρκὶ πεποιθότες Ep.Phil. 3.3 ; τὸν κύριον τῶν πνευμάτων καὶ πάσης ς. SIG 1181.3 (ii B.C., Jewish). (Perh. I.- E. twr[kcirc ]- 'portion', cf. Avest. θ war[schwa]s- 'cut'.)

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀνάλογος, ον, according to a due λόγος, proportionate, conformable, Pl. Ti. 69b , cf. Ti.Locr. 103d ; but ἐὰν τέσσαρα ἀνάλογα ᾖ in arithmetical progression, Ascl. Tact. 3.1 : neut. ἀνάλογον freq. in Arist. in adverbial sense, in proportion, EN 1158a35 , etc.; freq. as Adj., τὸ ἀνάλογον λέγω, ὅταν . . Po. 1457b16 ; παρὰ τὸ ἀ. EN 1131b11 , al., etc.; but ἐκ τοῦ ἀνάλογον Rh. 1399a33 , 1405a11 , al.; μεταφοραὶ αἱ ἀνάλογον (sc. οὖσαι) ib. 1408a8 ; τὰ τούτοις ἀνάλογον HA 487a5 , etc.; ἀ. οἰκοδόμοι (as a predicate) EN 1103b9 , cf. Rh. 1364b11 , al.:—so that it is plain that ἀνάλογον is merely equiv. to ἀνὰ λόγον, as it is written in Pl. Ti. 37a ; cf. λόγος:—the regul. Adv. ἀναλόγως Hp. Ep. 27 , LXX Wi. 13.5 , S.E. P. 1.88 , Alex.Aphr. in Metaph. 156.5 . well-proportioned, suitable, σχῆμα Philostr. Im. 1.10 ( Sup. ). equivalent to, resembling, λυπηρὸν ἢ ἀ. λυπηρῷ Phld. Ir. p.76W. , cf. Sign. 2 , 37 .

term_table.greek_sentence: κατὰ γοῦν τὸ σαρκῶδες γένος ἕτερος μὲν ὄγκος ὁ τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἐστιν, ἕτερος δὲ ὁ τῶν ὑγρῶν, ὥσπερ ἐρίου τινὸς ἢ σπογγιᾶς τῆς σαρκὸς ἐμπεπλησμένης ὑγρότητος περιττῆς· ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν τοιοῦτον πλῆθος ἐν ταῖς σαρξὶν ἀνάλογόν ἐστι τῷ κατὰ τὸ ἔγχυμα καλουμένῳ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀγγείων, τὸ δὲ ἕτερον πλῆθος τῷ πρὸς τὴν δύναμιν, ἢ μετὰ βάρους· μεμνημένων ἡμῶν, ὅτι μηδὲν διήνεγκεν, ἢ περὶ συνθέτου σαρκὸς, ἢ περὶ μυῶν διαλέγεσθαι, καὶ ὡς εἴ ποτε περὶ πλήθους ὁ λόγος γίγνοιτο τοῦ κατὰ τὰς σάρκας, τοὺς μῦς ἀκουστέον ἐστὶν, οὐ τὴν ἁπλῆν ἐκείνην σάρκα, τὴν ὑπό τινων ὀνομαζομένην παρέγχυμα.

term_table.greek_sentence: κατὰ μέντοι τὰς ἀρτηρίας καὶ τὰς φλέβας οὐχ ﻿ [573] ὁμοίως αἰσθητόν ἐστι τὸ πρὸς τὴν δύναμιν πλῆθος αὐτοῖς τοῖς κάμνουσιν, ἀλλ’ ὅσοι περ ἂν ὦσιν αἰσθητικώτατοι φύσει, μόνοις τοῖς τοιούτοις ἀμυδρόν τι καὶ βύθιον βάρος ἐμφαίνεται κατὰ τὸ σῶμα· διὸ χρὴ ζητεῖν ἕτερά τινα σαφέστερα τοῦ τοιούτου πλήθους γνωρίσματα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In the arteries and the veins, however, the plethora relative to the faculty is not [573] similarly perceptible to the patients themselves; rather, only in those who are by nature most sensitive does a certain faint and deep-seated heaviness make itself apparent throughout the body. Therefore one must seek certain other, clearer indications of such plethora.
term_table.english_sentence_B: In the arteries and veins, however, [573] the plethora relative to the strength is not perceptible in the same way to the patients themselves; rather, only to those who are by nature most sensitive does a faint and deep-seated heaviness appear in the body. Therefore one must seek certain other, clearer signs of such a plethora.

term_table.english_sentence_A: For in most cases the veins come into a state of plethora together with the arteries, on account of the confluence of the vessels, which we have often demonstrated elsewhere; but sometimes, when viscous or thick humours have accumulated in the veins, their transfer into the arteries does not come about easily — though such a case is rare; for unless the humours are extremely thick or viscous, they will in any case flow across.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For the most part the veins come into a state of plethora together with the arteries, on account of the confluence of the vessels, which we have often demonstrated in other works; but sometimes, when viscous or thick humours have collected in the veins, their transfer into the arteries does not take place readily. Such a thing, however, is rare; for unless the humours are extremely thick or viscous, they will certainly flow across.

term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ πολλὰ μὲν γὰρ ὁμοῦ ταῖς ἀρτηρίαις αἱ φλέβες ἐν πληθώρᾳ καθίστανται, διὰ τὴν σύῤῥοιαν τῶν ἀγγείων, ἣν πολλάκις ἐν ἑτέροις ἀπεδείξαμεν· ἔστιν ὅτε δὲ χυμῶν γλίσχρων, ἢ παχέων ἠσθροισμένων ἐν ταῖς φλεψὶν, οὐκ εὐπετὴς ἡ μετάληψις αὐτῶν εἰς τὰς ἀρτηρίας γίγνεται, σπάνιον δέ ἐστι τὸ τοιοῦτον· εἰ μὴ γὰρ ἐσχάτως εἶεν παχεῖς, ἢ γλίσχροι χυμοὶ, μεταῤῥυήσονται πάντως.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For in most cases the veins come into a state of plethora together with the arteries, on account of the confluence of the vessels, which we have often demonstrated elsewhere; but sometimes, when viscous or thick humours have accumulated in the veins, their transfer into the arteries does not come about easily — though such a case is rare; for unless the humours are extremely thick or viscous, they will in any case flow across.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For the most part the veins come into a state of plethora together with the arteries, on account of the confluence of the vessels, which we have often demonstrated in other works; but sometimes, when viscous or thick humours have collected in the veins, their transfer into the arteries does not take place readily. Such a thing, however, is rare; for unless the humours are extremely thick or viscous, they will certainly flow across.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἐν μὲν δὴ ταῖς τοιαύταις διαθέσεσιν οὐδὲν ἐναργὲς γνώρισμα τοῦ κατὰ τὰς φλέβας ἠθροισμένου πλήθους ἐκ (δὲ) τῆς τῶν ἀρτηριῶν κινήσεως ἔνεστι λαβεῖν, εἰ καὶ ὅτι μάλιστα τῷ Νικάρχῳ καὶ Πραξαγόρᾳ δοκεῖ, καίτοι μὴ μεταδιδοῦσι [574] ταῖς ἀρτηρίαις αἵματος· κατὰ μέντοι τὰς ἄλλας διαθέσεις τῆς πληθώρας πιστεύειν χρὴ τοῖς ἐκ τῶν σφυγμῶν σημείοις, ἃ διὰ τῆς οἰκείας εἴρηται πραγματείας, τὰς δὲ ἰδέας τοῦ πλήθους, ὅταν γε ὁμαλῶς ἐκτεταμένον εἰς ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ᾖ, κατὰ τάδε διαιρεῖσθαι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In such conditions, then, no clear sign of the plethos gathered in the veins can be obtained from the movement of the arteries, however much Nicarchus and Praxagoras may think so, even though they do not grant [574] the arteries any share of blood. term_table.lsj_entry_text: ὕπωχρος, ον, pale yellow, Arist. HA 586b33 , Dsc. 3.152 , Gal. 6.336 , 16.588 ; sallow, Hp. Int. 4 , Arist. Phgn. 807b7 , Philostr. Gym. 49 , Luc. Tox. 19 .
term_table.greek_sentence: ἐξέρυθρον μὲν γὰρ τὸ τοῦ αἵματος πλῆθός ἐστιν, ὕπωχρον δὲ τὸ τῆς ξανθῆς χολῆς, ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ λευκότερον ἐκτρέπεται τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν, ὅταν τὸ φλέγμα κρατῇ, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τὸ μελάντερον, ἢν ἡ μέλαινα χολή.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For the plethos of blood is deep red, that of yellow bile somewhat pale-yellow; and the colour turns toward whiter than the natural when phlegm predominates, just as toward darker if black bile does.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The kinds of plenitude, at least when it is evenly extended into the whole body, one must distinguish as follows. term_table.lsj_entry_text: λευκοφλεγματ-ία, ἡ, the beginning of dropsy (also called λευκὸν φλέγμα), dub. in Cels. 3.21 .
term_table.greek_sentence: μόνον δ’, εἴπερ ἄρα, τὸ φλέγμα, καὶ τοῦτο οὐχ ἅπαν ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ τὸ κατὰ τοὺς λευκοφλεγματίας ὀνομαζομένους ὑδέρους ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ σώματι δυνήσεται πλεονάσαι.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Only phlegm, if indeed anything, and this not every phlegm simply, but that found in the dropsies called leucophlegmatic, will be able to abound in the whole body.
term_table.english_sentence_B: It is clear that the so-called raw humour too must, at least in the present discussion, be counted as one of the kinds of phlegm; for if we shall posit it as different from that, then in addition to the differences of plethora we have just stated it is necessary to add also the one arising from such a humour. This humour is thicker than the other phlegm and less pneumatic, such as settles in urines, especially those which, as a result of gluttony, have a copious sediment resembling bean-pottage.

term_table.english_sentence_A: And it is clear that the humour called crude also must, in the present discussion at least, be set down as one of the kinds of phlegm; since if we posit it as something distinct from that, it is necessary to add, to the differentiae of plethora which we mentioned just now, also the one arising from such a humour. term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἁλυκ-ός, ή, όν, salt, Hp. Acut. 42 , Aër. 1 , Ar. Lys. 403 , LXX Ge. 14.3 ; brackish, Thphr. HP 4.3.5 .
term_table.greek_sentence: τὰ δ’ ἄλλα τοῦ φλέγματος εἴδη τὸ μέν [576] ἐστι γλυκὺ, τὸ δὲ ὀξὺ, τὸ δὲ ἁλυκόν· καὶ ὑπνώδεις μὲν γίνονται ἐπὶ τοῦ γλυκέος, πεινώδεις δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ ὀξέος πλεονάζοντος, ὥσπερ δὴ διψώδεις, ὅταν ἐπικρατῇ τὸ ἁλυκόν· ἀνόρεκτοι δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ προειρημένῳ τῷ ὠμῷ.
term_table.english_sentence_A: As for the other kinds of phlegm, one [576] is sweet, another sour, another salty; and people become somnolent when the sweet kind is in excess, hungry when the sour kind is in excess, just as they become thirsty when the salty kind prevails; and they become without appetite with the aforementioned raw humour.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Of the other kinds of phlegm, one [576] is sweet, another sour, another salty. term_table.english_sentence_A: As regards sleep, in the case of the other phlegms mentioned above it is a little more than what is in accordance with nature; but the raw humour, like the sweet phlegm, clearly renders people somnolent. term_table.english_sentence_A: For this reason, then, those who suffer from bile are all sleepless, with either of the two biles; and in the case of the black bile there is present in addition, as a distinctive feature, sullenness and despondency without reason.

term_table.greek_sentence: δῆλον δ’ ὅτι τὸ στόμα τῆς γαστρὸς εἴρηται νῦν στόμαχος, ἐν ᾧ τὸ μὲν φλέγμα τὸ ἀθροισθὲν, ὡς ὀλίγον ἔμπροσθεν εἴρηται, τὰς ὀρέξεις ἐποίησε· τῶν δὲ χολωδῶν, ἐπὶ μὲν τῆς ξανθῆς διψώδεις τε καὶ ἀσώδεις ἔσονται, καὶ τὸ στόμα πικρὸν αὐτοῖς ἐστιν· ἐπὶ δὲ τῇ μελαίνῃ, δύσθυμοι, καὶ σκυθρωποὶ, καὶ φοβεροὶ, καὶ ἄδιψοι, καὶ σιέλου μεστοὶ, ἀπόσιτοι δὲ οὐ πάντες, ἀλλά τινες αὐτῶν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: And it is clear that the mouth of the stomach has here been called stomachos, in which the phlegm that has gathered, as was said a little earlier, produced the appetites; but of the bilious humours, in the case of the yellow they will be thirsty and nauseous, and their mouth is bitter; whereas in the case of the black, they are despondent, sullen, fearful, without thirst, and full of saliva, but not all of them averse to food, only some of them.
term_table.english_sentence_B: It is clear that by 'stomach' (stomachos) is now meant the mouth of the belly (gastēr), in which the phlegm that has collected, as was said a little before, produced the appetites. Of the bilious, those with yellow bile will be thirsty and nauseated, and their mouth is bitter; those with black bile are despondent, sullen, fearful, free of thirst and full of saliva; not all of them are averse to food, but some of them are.

term_table.english_sentence_A: But so long as it is merely like a sediment of blood, and not yet precisely acid, it is perhaps better (so far as it is called a melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile either, but, as I am accustomed, melancholic, because it has come near to becoming black bile.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἀλλ’ οὐ νῦν καιρὸς ὑπὲρ τῆς ἐν ταῖς κακοχυμίαις διεξέρχεσθαι διαφορᾶς, ὅτι μηδὲ πλῆθος εἶπον ὀνομάζεσθαι αὐτάς· ἡμῖν δὲ οὐχ ἁπλῶς τὸ πλεονάζον ὁπωσοῦν ἐξευρεῖν, ἀλλὰ περὶ πλήθους ﻿ [578] σκέψασθαι προὔκειτο· πλεονεξία δέ ἐστι τοῦτο τῶν καθ’ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα τοῦ ζώου χυμῶν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: But now is not the occasion to go through the difference among the cacochymiai, since I said that they are not even called plethos; for our proposed task was not simply to discover what is in excess in whatever manner, but to inquire about plethos; [578] and this is an excess of the humours throughout the whole body of the animal.
term_table.english_sentence_B: But this is not the time to go through the differences among the cacochymias, since I said that they are not even called plenitude. Our proposed task was not simply to find out whatever is in excess in any way whatsoever, but to examine plenitude [578]; and this is an excess of the humours throughout the whole body of the animal.

term_table.english_sentence_A: One ought not, then, to desire to hear in this discourse about the forms either of the local swellings or of cacochymia, but about when either all the humours are increased according to their original proportion, or one of them acquires some slight preponderance.

term_table.greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν οὖν αἷμα παμπόλλην ὑπεροχὴν δύναται λαβεῖν ἐν ταῖς πληθωρικαῖς διαθέσεσι, τῶν δὲ ἄλλων χυμῶν οὐδείς· κακοχυμία γὰρ ἤδη τό γε τοιοῦτον, οὐκ ἔτι πλῆθος, οὐδὲ πληθώρα καλεῖται.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Now blood can acquire a very great preponderance in the plethoric dispositions, but none of the other humours can; for such a thing is already cacochymia, and is no longer called plethos, nor plethora.

term_table.greek_sentence: διὸ καὶ σφυγμοὶ κατὰ μὲν τὰς κακοχυμίας οἰκεῖοι τῇ φύσει τῶν χυμῶν ἀκριβῶς εἰσιν· ἐπὶ δὲ τοῖς εἰρημένοις πλήθεσιν οὐχ ὁμοίως ἐναργεῖς ἀποσώζουσι τὰς διαφορὰς, ὅτι σὺν αἵματι δαψιλεῖ πάντως ἐστὶν ὁ πλεονάζων χυμός· ὅταν δὲ κρατήσῃ σφοδρῶς, ἐπὶ μὲν τῇ ξανθῇ χολῇ τοιούτους ἀνάγκη γενέσθαι σφυγμοὺς, οἵους εἴπομεν ἕπεσθαι, ξηραινομένης τε καὶ θερμαινομένη τῆς καρδίας· ἐπὶ δὲ τῇ μελαίνῃ τοιούτους αὖ πάλιν, οἵους ἔφαμεν, εἰ ψύχοιτό τε καὶ ξηραίνοιτο, γίγνεσθαι· κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν [579] λόγον, εἰ νικήσειέν ποτε τὸ φλέγμα τοὺς ἄλλους, ψυχρᾶς καὶ ὑγρᾶς διαθέσεως ἐκγόνους ἀποτελέσει σφυγμούς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Hence also the pulses in the cacochymias are precisely proper to the nature of the humours; but in the cases of plethos that have been mentioned they do not preserve their differences with equal clarity, because the humour that is in excess is in every case accompanied by abundant blood. But when it prevails strongly, in the case of yellow bile the pulses must necessarily become such as we said follow when the heart is being dried and heated; and in the case of black bile, such in turn as we said arise if it is cooled and dried; and by the same [579] reasoning, if phlegm should ever overcome the others, it will produce pulses that are the offspring of a cold and moist disposition.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For this reason the pulses too, in cacochymias, are precisely proper to the nature of the humours; but in the plethoras mentioned they do not preserve their differences equally clearly, because the humour that is in excess is in every case together with abundant blood. But when it prevails strongly, with yellow bile the pulses must necessarily become such as we said follow when the heart is dried and heated; with black bile, in turn, such as we stated arise if it should be cooled and dried; and by the same [579] reasoning, if phlegm should ever overcome the others, it will produce pulses that are the offspring of a cold and moist condition.

term_table.greek_sentence: αἵματι δὲ τῷ μὲν ἀκριβῶς κατὰ φύσιν οὐδεμία τῆς ἀρχαίας καταστάσεως ἀλλοίωσις ἕπεται· τῷ δὲ ὑγροτέρῳ πλεονάζοντι καὶ οἱ σφυγμοὶ συναλλοιοῦνται, καθάπερ εἰ θερμότερόν τε καὶ ψυχρότερον ἑαυτοῦ γένοιτο.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Upon blood that is precisely in accordance with nature no alteration of the original condition follows; but when moister blood is in excess, the pulses too are altered along with it, just as if it should become hotter or colder than itself.
term_table.english_sentence_B: With blood that is exactly in accordance with nature no alteration of the original state follows; but when blood that is moister is in excess, the pulses too are altered along with it, just as if it should become hotter or colder than itself.

term_table.greek_sentence: αἵματι δὲ τῷ μὲν ἀκριβῶς κατὰ φύσιν οὐδεμία τῆς ἀρχαίας καταστάσεως ἀλλοίωσις ἕπεται· τῷ δὲ ὑγροτέρῳ πλεονάζοντι καὶ οἱ σφυγμοὶ συναλλοιοῦνται, καθάπερ εἰ θερμότερόν τε καὶ ψυχρότερον ἑαυτοῦ γένοιτο.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Upon blood that is precisely in accordance with nature no alteration of the original condition follows; but when moister blood is in excess, the pulses too are altered along with it, just as if it should become hotter or colder than itself.

term_table.english_sentence_A: And indeed also by way of conjunction it will be rendered moister and colder, or colder and drier, hotter and moister, or hotter and drier, in consequence of the aforementioned [580] causes, without any one of the other humours having gained the upper hand.

term_table.english_sentence_B: But if it should also arrive at a dyscrasia through the mixture of those humours, such a dyscrasia would be constituted together with cacochymia. term_table.greek_sentence: οἱ σφυγμοὶ δὲ κατὰ τὰς δυσκρασίας τὰς ὀκτὼ τὴν ἰδέαν ἐκείνην ἕξουσιν, οἵαν ἐν τῇ τῶν σφυγμῶν πραγματείᾳ διήλθομεν· εἴτε δ’, ὡς εἵρηται, μόνου τοῦ αἵματός ἐστιν, εἴτε διά τινα ἐπιμιξίαν χυμοῦ, διορίζεσθαι χρὴ τῇ τε συνούσῃ χρόᾳ παντὸς τοῦ σώματος καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις συμπτώμασιν, ὅσα περὶ ὕπνου καὶ ἐγρηγόρσεως, ἢ ὀρέξεως καὶ ἀνορεξίας, ἢ εἴτι τοιοῦτον, μικρὸν ἔμπροσθεν εἴρηται, καὶ τῇ προηγησαμένῃ διαίτῃ, καὶ τοῖς γυμνασίοις, καὶ τοῖς αὐτῷ τῷ κάμνοντι συμπίπτειν εἰθισμένοις, ἔτι τε τῇ ὥρᾳ καὶ τῇ χώρᾳ καὶ τῇ φυσικῇ πυκνότητι καὶ ἀραιότητι τοῦ σώματος· ἄμεινον γὰρ ἐκ πάντων τὸ πιστὸν τῇ διαγνώσει λαμβάνειν, οὐκ ἐξ ἑνὸς ἢ δυοῖν, εὖ εἰδότας ὡς αὐτὸ μόνον ἐν τῇ [581] τέχνῃ πλεῖστα κεκοινώνηκε τοῦ στοχάζεσθαι, λέγω δὴ τὸ μέρος τῆς τέχνης τοῦτο τὸ διαγνωστικὸν ἅπαν, οὐ μόνον τὸ κατὰ τὴν κακοχυμίαν, ἢ τὸ πλῆθος, ἃ νῦν ἡμῖν διορίζεσθαι πρόκειται· τὰ γὰρ περὶ τὰς ἐνεργείας, ἢ τὰς τῶν νοσημάτων αἰτίας, ἢ τὰς ἰάσεις, ἐπιστημονικώτερον ἔχει τὴν γνῶσιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: The pulses, in accordance with the eight dyscrasias, will have that form which we went through in the treatise on the pulses; and whether, as has been said, it belongs to the blood alone, or is due to some admixture of a humour, one must distinguish by the colour accompanying the whole body and by the other symptoms—as many as have been mentioned a little earlier concerning sleep and wakefulness, or appetite and lack of appetite, or anything else of the kind—and by the regimen that has preceded, and the exercises, and the things that habitually befall the patient himself, and further by the season and the region and the natural density and rarity of the body; for it is better to take the assurance for the diagnosis from all of these, not from one or two, knowing well that this alone in the [581] art has the greatest share in conjecture—I mean this whole diagnostic part of the art, not only that which concerns cacochymia or plethos, which it is now our task to distinguish; for the matters concerning the activities, or the causes of diseases, or the cures, have a knowledge that is more scientific.
term_table.english_sentence_B: The pulses in the eight dyscrasias will have that form which we set out in the treatise on pulses. Whether, as has been said, it belongs to the blood alone, or arises from some admixture of a humour, one must determine by the accompanying colour of the whole body and by the other symptoms (those concerning sleep and waking, or appetite and lack of appetite, or anything of that kind, which were stated a little earlier), and by the preceding regimen, and the exercises, and the things that are accustomed to befall the patient himself, and further by the season and the country and the natural density and rarity of the body.

Caes. 9 , Cic. 19 . of things, good, serviceable, Ἰθάκη . . ἀ. κουροτρόφος Od. 9.27 , etc.; ἀ. τοῖς τοκεῦσι, τῇ πόλει X. Cyn. 13.17 : c. gen., εἴ τι οἶδα πυρετοῦ ἀ. good for it, Id. HP 9.11.1 . of outward circumstances, αἰδὼς οὐκ ἀ. κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι Od. 17.347 ; εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν to good purpose, Il. 9.102 ; ὁ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀ. περ for his own good end, 11.789 ; οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη 2.204 :—ἀγαθόν [ἐστι], c. inf., it is good to do so and so<*> Il. 7.282 , 24.130 , Od. 3.196 , etc. morally good, πρῆξις Democr. 177 ; ἔργα Emp. 112.2 , cf. Ep.Rom. 2.7 , etc. ἀγαθόν, τό, good, blessing, benefit, of persons or things, ὦ μέγα ἀ. σὺ τοῖς φίλοις X. Cyr. 5.3.20 ; φίλον, ὃ μέγιστον ἀ. εἶναί φασι Id. Mem. 2.4.2 , cf. Ar. Ra. 74 , etc; as term of endearment for a baby, blessing!, treasure!, Men. term_table.greek_sentence: σκεπτέον οὖν, εἰ μηδὲν τούτῳ τῶν θερμαινόντων αἰτίων ἐπλησίασεν· εἰ γάρ τοι φαίνοιτο, βέλτιον ἀναβάλλεσθαι τὴν διάγνωσιν, ἄχρι περ ἂν ἡ ἐξ ἐκείνου κίνησις ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ σώματι καταστῇ, διότι μήτε θυμούμενον, ἢ λελουμένον, ἢ λουόμενον, ἢ γεγυμνασμένον, ἢ οἴνου προσενηνεγμένον ἀρτίως, ἢ ἄλλως ὁπωσοῦν τεθερμασμένον εἰς τὴν διάγνωσιν ἄγειν προσήκει, ἀλλ’ ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ πασῶν τῶν ἔξωθεν ὑπάρχοντα κινήσεων· εἰ γὰρ ἐν ἐκείνῳ [582] τῷ καιρῷ φαίνοιτο τοιοῦτος, αἷμα πλεονάζει τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ.
term_table.english_sentence_A: One must therefore consider whether none of the heating causes has come near this man; for if it should appear that one has, it is better to postpone the diagnosis until the movement arising from that cause has settled down throughout the whole body, since it is not fitting to bring to diagnosis a man who is angry, or has bathed, or is bathing, or has exercised, or has just taken wine, or has been heated in any other way whatsoever, but one who is at rest from all external movements; for if at that [582] time he should appear of this sort, blood is in excess in the man.
term_table.english_sentence_B: One must therefore consider whether any of the heating causes has come near him; for if one should appear to have done so, it is better to postpone the diagnosis until the motion arising from it has settled down in the whole body, since it is not proper to bring to diagnosis someone who is angry, or has bathed, or is bathing, or has exercised, or has just taken wine, or has been heated in any other way whatsoever, but rather one who is at rest from all external motions. For if at that [582] time he should appear such, blood is in excess in the person.

term_table.greek_sentence: τοὐντεῦθεν ἐπισκέπτεσθαι τἄλλα, πρῶτα μὲν ὅσα μεγίστην ἔχει δύναμιν, εἶτα ἑξῆς τὰ λοιπά· ἐδείχθη δὲ βάρος καὶ τάσις, ὅ τε πρὸς τὰς κινήσεις ὄκνος, εἶθ’ ἑξῆς τὰ κατὰ τοὺς σφυγμοὺς, ἀγρυπνίας τε καὶ ὕπνους, ὀρέξεις τε καὶ ἀνορεξίας, ὅσα τ’ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα.
term_table.english_sentence_A: From there one should examine the other signs, first those that have the greatest force, then the rest in order; it was shown that heaviness and tension have this, and the reluctance towards movements, then next the matters pertaining to the pulses, wakefulness and sleep, appetites and lack of appetite, and whatever other things are of this kind.
term_table.english_sentence_B: From there one should examine the other signs, first those that have the greatest force, then the rest in order. It was shown that these are heaviness and tension, and reluctance towards movements, and then next the features of the pulses, sleeplessness and sleep, appetites and lack of appetite, and whatever other things are of this kind.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔκ-κρισις, εως, ἡ, separation, Arist. Mete. 342a15 , Onos. 9.1 (pl.). secretion, of the animal functions, Arist. PA 689a16 , GA 727a2 ; τῶν ὑγρῶν Eun. Hist. p.263 D. = ἔκκριμα , of excrement, Hp. Aph. 2.15 ; of the menses, Arist. HA 583a2 , etc.
term_table.greek_sentence: μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα τῶν προηγησαμένων ἕκαστον, ὅσα πλῆθος ἐργάζεται, μή τις συνήθης ἔκκρισις ἐπέσχηται, μὴ γυμνάσιον ἠμέληται, μὴ πλείω καὶ πολύτροφα σιτία συνεχῶς προσενήνεκται, μὴ μετὰ τροφὴν ἀήθεσι χρῆται λουτροῖς, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἔτι μὴ πολλάκις ὁ τοιοῦτος ἄνθρωπος ἁλίσκεται νοσήμασι πληθωρικοῖς.
term_table.english_sentence_A: After these, each of the antecedent causes that produce plethos: whether some customary excretion has been held back, whether exercise has been neglected, whether foods in greater quantity and highly nourishing have been taken continually, whether he makes use of unaccustomed baths after food, and in addition to these, further, whether such a man is frequently seized by plethoric diseases.
term_table.english_sentence_B: After these, each of the antecedent factors that produce plethora: whether some habitual excretion has been suppressed, whether exercise has been neglected, whether larger quantities of highly nourishing foods have been taken continually, whether he makes use of unaccustomed baths after food, and in addition to these, whether such a person is frequently seized by plethoric diseases.

term_table.greek_sentence: ἐπὶ τούτοις ἅπασι καὶ τὰ παρὰ τῆς χώρας, καὶ ὥρας, ἢ εἴτι τοιοῦτον ἄλλο προσθεὶς, οὐκ ἴσην ἅπασι νέμων τὴν αἰτίαν, ὥσπερ οὐδ’ ἐν τοῖς ἄλλοις μέρεσι τῆς τέχνης· ἔνια μὲν γὰρ τῶν γνωρισμάτων ἐστὶν ἐπιστημονικὰ, καθάπερ ἡ τάσις, καὶ τὸ βάρος, ὅ τε ὄγκος τῶν φλεβῶν, ὅ τε ὄκνος, καὶ τὸ χρῶμα, καὶ ἡ τῶν σφυγμῶν κίνησις, ἁπασῶν δηλονότι τῶν προσφάτων κινήσεων ἀφωρισμένων· ἔνια δὲ ἀπολείπεται τούτων, οἷον ἡ τῶν, ἐκκρίσεων [583] ἐπίσχεσις, ὅ τε ἀργὸς βίος, ἐδέσματά τε πλείω καὶ τρόφιμα, καὶ μετὰ τροφὴν λουτρά· συνιόντα μέντοι τὰ σύμπαντα τοῖς ἐπιστημονικοῖς ἐγγὺς ἥκει.
term_table.english_sentence_A: In addition to all these, adding also the factors deriving from the region and the season, or anything else of this kind, not assigning an equal share of causation to all, just as one does not in the other parts of the art either; for some of the signs are scientific, such as tension, heaviness, the swelling of the veins, reluctance, the colour, and the movement of the pulses—all recent movements, of course, having been set aside; but some fall short of these, such as the suppression of the excretions, [583] an idle life, foods more abundant and more nourishing, and baths after food; yet when all of these come together they come close to the scientific ones.
term_table.english_sentence_B: On top of all these, one adds also the indications from the region and the season, or anything else of this kind, without assigning equal importance to all of them, just as one does not in the other parts of the art either. For some of the signs are scientific, such as the tension, the heaviness, the swelling of the veins, the reluctance [to move], the colour, and the movement of the pulses, provided, obviously, that all recent motions have been excluded.

A.translation: [513] GALEN'S BOOK ON PLETHORA. One cannot find practically all the physicians of the present day either naming any other term more often than plethora, or being more ignorant of anything else than of this. At any rate, of those among them who are capable both of giving and of receiving an account, the majority reply to those who ask them what exactly it is that they call plethora, that the name is used among the relatives, just like "much" and "little," so that it is not possible to comprehend it within a measure; for what is much for one thing, this is sometimes less for another.

And when you ask them, demanding that they answer what the thing is in relation to which the plethora exists, as [514] they say, some become more voiceless than fish, while others talk such long-winded and bizarre nonsense that one cannot follow what is said by them. Very few answer that the much and the little are understood in relation to the faculty; and if you were to question them again in turn as to what they mean by 'faculty', some do not answer at all, while of those who venture to declare something, no one says the same thing as any other, and most interpret it as anything rather than a faculty. And if someone among them should be found prudent to such a degree as to say that the faculty is either an active substance or an active cause, and should then be asked, first whether there is any such substance governing the animal, and then, if there is, to explain what in the world it is, this man too no longer answers the point in question when asked it, but either falls completely silent or diverts the argument into such a form that it would be better to be silent.

But if even among these someone should be found sensible to such a degree as to say that he cannot state what the substance of the faculty is, but that it exists he infers from its works, this very man too, in his turn, when asked whether he has examined and refuted the things written [515] by Asclepiades and by many Asclepiadeans and Methodics to the effect that there is no faculty at all in animals, appears not even to know whether anything has been said by them. And of those themselves, again, as many as say that the faculty does not exist, it is all the more evident that they deny that plethora is conceived and constituted in relation to this; for it is impossible for plethora to be constituted and conceived in a relation to what does not exist at all; rather, they suppose that much and little exist only in relation to the spaces of the vessels; and sometimes they do not even use the name plethora at all in the first place, nor do they take from it any indication for evacuation, but only from constriction, which, as has been shown elsewhere, no one of them explains in the same way.

And indeed there is also a third, further band, which neither knows whether there is or is not some faculty, nor admits to inquiring into it, but asserts that, on the basis of certain clearly apparent signs which come together in the patient, the evacuation has been discovered by itself from long experience; then, when asked what exactly [516] these signs are, it says distension of the vessels, and redness and heaviness of the whole body, and reluctance toward movements, and tensions of the limbs. Some of them add also the ulcerous and lassitude-like sensation, and an idle previous manner of life amid rather abundant intakes of foods and drinks, and the suppression of customary excretions. Upon this syndrome, at any rate—for so they call the aggregate of symptoms—phlebotomy has been observed to be beneficial. These men, then, deprive not only themselves but also all other human beings of reason, asserting that everything has been discovered from experience; while the others, as has just now been said, say that they use reason, and as for the faculty, some say that it does not exist at all, others that it exists, but that what its substance is is not known; so that very few are those who dare to declare both the existence and the substance of a faculty.

But even among these, not all declare the same number or the same substance; rather, even of those who have left us writings, some rather carelessly always discourse as about a single power that governs the animal, [517] adding no reasoning, while some attempt to demonstrate it, and say that there are not more than one. So it is necessary that whoever declares there to be plethora in the body of the patient has already separated himself both from the physicians called Empiricists and from the Methodists, and that he speaks of "much" either in relation to the power or in relation to the vessels. Accordingly, let our discussion against the Empiricists and Methodists be postponed, and let us proceed to the others, all those who say that they practise the art with reasoning. And yet some of those of the present day have come to such a pitch of audacity as to inscribe upon themselves the names of a sect, while knowing nothing even of those very doctrines (ἐστὶν). At any rate one may often hear many of them, in the presence of the sick, saying that the man is full and must be phlebotomised, and then again, when discussion arises, calling themselves Methodists or Empiricists. But, as I was saying, having come to those who employ analogism, let us converse first with those among them who always conceive "much" in relation to the power.

For these men run the risk [518] of never having seen wineskins or sacks filled beyond measure, nor indeed of ever having taken more food than is required, so as to distend the belly, nor of ever having accumulated urine in the bladder beyond what is proper, or excrement in the rectum; for in all such circumstances each of the organs mentioned is manifestly distended, so that the person is distressed unless he quickly excretes the excess. Nor indeed is the sensation the same of what weighs down, or of what bites, or of what causes distress by some indescribable quality. At any rate one can hear even laymen clearly describing the very thing that is happening to them, without any contentiousness about doctrine: sometimes that they are weighed down and oppressed by food, even though they have taken very little; sometimes that they are being bitten and gnawed; and often, being unable to describe accurately what is happening, they say that they are nauseated (ἀσᾶσθαι). For none of these sensations is the same in people (πρὸς τοῖς ἀνθρώποις) when the belly has been stretched and distended to the greatest extent because of an immoderate quantity of foods.

In such states, then, they say that their belly is in danger [519] of bursting, and at the same time we too see it stretched to the utmost; but where they say they are weighed down, we sometimes see the stomach drawn in. So too in the case of the bladder, there is one disposition when it contains a very great quantity of fluid, and another when it contains little, or is weighed down. And accordingly one can see that the excretion, in the case of the bladder that is stretched because it has been filled, is very copious, whereas in the case of the one that is weighed down it is very scanty, but very frequent; for it does not wait for the time of filling, but at once longs to cast off what distresses it, just as also when it is bitten by the quality of the fluid. For then too it makes the excretion continuous. And so indeed, whenever it is weighed down, as if by a burden, by what it contains, then one could not rightly say that it is merely in a bad condition, but rather that what weighs it down is much for it, even if it does not distend its tunic at all.

But as for these matters, whatever the leaders of this opinion may say, since those who hold the contrary views deny it, both parties must again be asked whether the bladder suffers the same distress when it is distended in every direction and in danger [520] of bursting, because it can no longer contain what is held within it, and when it is weighed down and bitten. For here again those who always conceive plethora in relation to the roominess of the vessels readily concede it; whereas those who conceive it in relation to the faculty are vexed at such questions and grow angry, resisting in manifold ways, up and down, because they are unwilling to concede that this too is plethora. We, then, having prayed that both parties cease from their contentiousness, called them to concord: those who think that plethora is never spoken of in relation to the space of the container—and with these indeed we first began our discussion—we exhorted to yield to the truth, recalling that the parts which have been filled are pained in being distended; and those who think that plethora is constituted in this way only, to concede that that which weighs down is much for that which is weighed down.

And again, putting each party to shame by means of what is evidently apparent, let us remind separately those who assert that 'much' is conceived only in relation to the power, of the peritoneum being ruptured or dilated (ἀνευρυνθέντες) by a plethora of foods, and let us point out that among external things too wineskins and bladders [521] suffer this, and sometimes even the storage jars themselves, when the plethora is pneumatic and violent. And let us ask about those who have coughed up blood from the lung, and that through the rupture of a vessel, without a blow, or a fall, or any other such violence from outside, whether these too do not seem to them to have suffered in this way from a very great plethora distending the vessel. And separately, in turn, let us remind the others that a young man in good condition and a quite small child cannot carry the same weight; for what, I suppose, is heaviest for the child is lightest for the young man. Shall we then say that what someone cannot carry is not a burden at all, nor that what thus weighs down is much? Or shall we grant that it is a burden and heavy, but not allow it to be called plethora? But in that case the dispute will be not about a matter of fact but about a name. And in the other case, one who says that he is never weighed down at all, not even if you place twenty talents on his shoulder, would not seem to you even to be a human being. But against those who have subjected themselves to a slavish doctrine nothing is sufficient.

So, leaving these men aside now—or rather, if the truth [522] must be told, bidding them depart—let us converse with whoever is free and a companion of truth. For we posited two notions and relations of plethora: the one in relation to the strength and power of that which bears it, the other in relation to the space that receives it. And having posited these things, let us examine how many in all the faculties of the animal are, and how we shall either recognise or treat the plethora in respect of each of them; and in addition to these, further, how many in total the kinds are of the humours themselves, either of those that weigh down the faculty or of those that are not contained within the vessels. For it is in these matters that the physician ought to be industrious and great, not in despising the evident things, which are the principles of every demonstration. But perhaps it is no wonder that this very thing too is unknown to those who have investigated nothing concerning demonstration, who have neither discovered it, nor learned it, nor practised it.

At any rate they are so simple-minded that even now someone who takes up these writings expects, first, that I should demonstrate in this discourse the things which anyone who intends to investigate anything about plethora [523] accurately must by all means know; and second, that I should discover the diagnosis and treatment of each kind of plethora — not recognising that, if matters so great were of such a nature as to be demonstrated through a single writing, the art would not be long. But I, for my part, have demonstrated in the books On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato that the faculty in the arteries is something other than that in the nerves and veins. And through the same treatise I also taught that the heart is, as it were, a kind of source of the faculty of the arteries, the brain of that of the nerves, and the liver of that of the veins. And in the book On the Elements according to Hippocrates I demonstrated that the substance underlying generation and corruption is altered throughout the whole of itself according to the four qualities, moisture and dryness, heat and cold, and that the proper substance of each of the bodies lies in a particular mixture of these, and that for this reason also the peculiar character of the mixture is the substance of the faculties that govern them. This has also been shown by me in the book On the Natural Faculties, and separately through a certain other treatise.

Diagnostic signs, too, have already been stated many times in many [524] treatises, both of each of the two kinds of plethora and of each of the species under either kind individually. By "each of the two" I mean the one relative to the faculty and the one according to the filling (enchyma); for this is what they call the other kind of plethora, the one which is measured by the containing space, and which arises not only in animals but no less in inanimate things as well, in woven fabrics and plaited work, in skins, and in vessels of earthenware and of bronze and of iron, and all those that are made of bronze and silver and tin. For these too burst when a great quantity of pneumatic substance has been shut up within them—unless indeed someone should wish to hold that even such a plethora is constituted in relation to the cohesive faculty, forgetting the notion we mentioned at the beginning in connection with the name "faculty", when we said that it is an active cause, on the ground that it makes no difference whether one says "active" or "efficient".

Nor, if someone should wish to say that the faculty is a substance and not an efficient cause, do we contradict him; we wish only this to be preserved in the argument, that the faculty be said to be active and efficient, and not passive and material, whether [525] it be a cause or a substance. For if this at least is preserved, it is evident that the faculty will be the cause of some activity; and the activity must surely itself be a motion from the agent into the patient, just as the affection too is the motion in the patient (deriving) from the agent (εἰς τὸ πάσχον, "into the patient"); so that the conception of the faculty lies in the category of the relative, and its existence in its relation to something else. But to say that anything whatever acts upon itself, or exercises its activity upon itself, is contrary to the notion; and so likewise to say that it holds itself together. For indeed those who above all introduced the cohesive faculty, such as the Stoics, make that which holds together one thing and that which is held together another: for they make the pneumatic substance that which holds together, and the material substance that which is held together; whence they say that air and fire hold together, while earth and water are held together.

And yet some of those who nowadays call themselves Herophileans, having not even in a dream heard these things, boldly make pronouncements about the cohesive faculty: confessing that they do not know whether it is air, or fire, or the combination of both, that holds together stones and pieces of wood and all other things of this kind; [526] but declaring simply that it is some faculty that holds together all such things, for they would be dissolved and flow apart if nothing were drawing them together and binding them tight; then, when asked whether they also dare to employ in the argument an axiom of this sort, namely that all existing things need something that holds them together, or not, they at once readily make the pronouncement and answer the question in the affirmative; but when led from there to an absurdity, they retract what has been said, and are indignant with their questioners as busybodies and sophists. For this, if anything, has been practised by the physicians of today: to make pronouncements readily about the greatest doctrines, but, when refuted, to be vexed and to call those who refute them sophists. How, then, it is necessary for the argument to be led into something absurd, once we have posited that every existing thing needs a cohesive cause, I shall now go through for you. The cohesive cause, whatever it is—for the Herophileans do not admit that they know it—do they themselves suppose it to be one of the things that exist, or of the things that do not exist?

For if it is something among the things that are not, I marvel at the [527] wisdom of these men, if they say that each of the things that are stands in need of something among the things that are not; but if they posit the containing cause among the things that are, let them recall that they said that everything that is needs a containing cause in order to be. For in this way it will follow that the cause itself also needs another cause in order to exist, and that one in turn another, and so on to infinity. But if they say that some of the things that are need some other cause for their being, while others have their being from themselves, first let them know that they are no longer preserving the original axiom, which they declared to be true above all else, that everything that is needs a containing cause in order to be; and second, that they require a very long argument as to why some things need it and others do not, and also which among them each of these two kinds is. For neither do the majority of the Herophileans, nor the more recent Stoics, state any demonstration of the claim that pneuma and fire hold together both themselves and the other things, whereas water and earth need something else to hold them together.

For, so far as the ready appearance goes, what is hard and resistant and dense would be said to hold itself together, while what is rare [528] and soft and yielding would be said to need something else to hold it together. And not only do these men, having stated no demonstration, think it right that their hypothesis be believed, but they also no longer perceive that in positing it they make it conflict with itself. For the things that are finest in their particles and softest and most yielding of all, fire and air—these, they say, are the causes for earth of its hardness and resistance, as though it were possible for one thing to impart to another some power, or nature, or activity, or quality of which it itself has no share. And indeed, moreover, it is clearly evident not only that nothing is held together by fire, but also that all things are dissolved by it. Against the hypothesis of the Stoics, then, I have spoken at greater length elsewhere; but I return to the Herophileans, and against these it will suffice me, for the present at least, to say that their leader has been affected in the most contrary way: he is at a loss in very many matters that have ready demonstrations, yet pronounces confidently in others whose demonstrations are impossible and whose hypothesis is false.

[529] Leaving these men too aside, then, let us say once more that being distended and being ruptured on account of plethora is an affection of the containing vessels themselves, not of some faculty; whereas being weighed down is an affection of a sensitive faculty—for not even this is, simply, an affection of every faculty whatsoever; at any rate, being weighed down is not an affection of the natural faculty. If, then, we demonstrated correctly in the treatise On the Natural Faculties that one faculty is attractive of what is proper, another alterative of these same things, another a retentive faculty, and a fourth expulsive of what is foreign, one must seek certain other signs of the plethora relative to each of the faculties mentioned, since heaviness is not sufficient. For it is not the case that, just as the weak stomach perceives the things that weigh it down, owing to its exceptional degree of sensation, so too the vein and the artery have the same sensation; rather, they have a different one. If indeed, then, the kind (γένος) is not the same in respect of the nerves (κατὰ τὰ νεῦρα)—a matter requiring a longer discussion for its exposition and proof.

Now of the plethora in the arteries, considered in relation to their faculty, scientific indications [530] have been stated in the treatise on the pulses; yet those who so readily speak of plethora every day know none of these things either. But of the plethora relative to the veins I have neither myself discovered any scientific sign, nor been able to find one written in another author, seeing that no one before us has even, to begin with, defined scientifically the faculties themselves. For Philippus and Archigenes and their followers touched to a small extent upon the theory of them, but none even of these worked it out completely. The present discussion inquires, however, not only into these matters but also into the plethora in each individual part, such as that in the liver, or heart, or kidneys, or colon, or brain, or bone. Now as many of them as are either difficult of sensation or insensible — these would not be sensible (αἰσθητὰ) in the same way as the stomach and bladder are of the superfluities in them, but some not at all, others either altogether faintly or not at all: altogether faintly, as in the case of a very great plethora, and not at all, as in the case of a small one.

For indeed a sensation of heaviness sometimes arises in the lung and the liver and the kidneys, and someone has perceived a bone being weighed down, he too with a faint sensation; in the [531] brain, however, heaviness often gives signs that are not only not faint but sometimes even quite clear. In the insensitive parts, on the other hand, no sensation can arise, either of heaviness or of any other symptom whatever; and some of the bones seem to be insensitive, and the fat, and some of the glands, unless indeed all the marrows too belong to the insensitive parts; at any rate the brain and the spinal marrow, as some say, belong to the sensitive ones. One could pronounce with confidence against the flesh around the convex parts of the liver, which the majority of physicians call parenchyma; for no nerve at all is implanted in it from anywhere; but one might be at a loss also concerning the flesh in the concave parts. For the nerves implanted in the liver at the portae are so short that they appear to interweave only its membrane.

And indeed one might raise the same difficulty with regard to the spleen and the kidneys likewise, and still more in the case of the lung; and perhaps, if there is any sensation of heaviness in these viscera, it might be said to belong not to the viscera themselves but to the tunics and membranes that surround them, and especially in the case of the lung and [532] the liver, which are attached and suspended, and not firmly fixed in place. For sufferers often clearly perceive a certain tension above, near the collar-bone, as in the case of swellings in the liver, when the viscus itself is heavy; and how fortunate is anyone who has not perceived this in the whole course of his life, seeing that it occurs so continually in everyone. And Hippocrates too says somewhere, 'into the kidney a heavy pain', just as heaviness also arises in the lung; and this has been stated by almost all physicians, whenever the viscus is seized by inflammation. But most physicians, having investigated none of these matters—and some not even the fact that plethora can sometimes be throughout the whole animal, but may also be about any single part whatsoever, or even several—pronounce rashly concerning plethora. But if you wish, let us for the present leave aside all these difficulties and exercise ourselves in the more tractable matters. And it seems to me more tractable to begin again from heaviness; for this appears to be the most evident sign of the plethora relative to the sensitive faculty.

Is it, [533] then, true to declare that heaviness follows plethora of necessity, or that heaviness necessarily precedes plethora? For it is certainly not the same thing whether heaviness follows in the proposition or precedes. For it is true that whoever has a plethora of certain fluids in the body, that person has a sensation of heaviness—obviously in those parts in which the plethora is present, these being sensitive parts; but it is not true that, when heaviness is present in some part, there is a plethora of humours in that part. For it is possible for the faculty, when it is weak, to be weighed down by the solid parts, as in paralyses. For since (τῆς) a whole limb is moved by the muscles (ἐν), when the muscles become too weak to move it and carry it from place to place, a sensation of heaviness arises in those who are paralysed.

For what is weak does not appear heavy to itself—for example the muscle, or the nerve, or in general whatever body it is that primarily moves the parts—but this affection which is called heaviness naturally arises in one thing from another; and the nerve itself by itself, or the tendon, or the muscle, or whatever it is that moves us, can indeed become more lacking in tone [534] and weaker than it was, but to weigh itself down is among the things impossible. When, then, it becomes better in tone, it will produce activities stronger than before; when more lacking in tone, weaker ones. For example the muscle, if indeed it is this that moves the leg, when healthy will draw vigorously that part of the limb into which it is inserted, when in good condition most vigorously, and when diseased, weakly, and when it is enfeebled in its power, faintly. But if it is not the muscle, but rather the nerve that moves the muscle itself, then in turn the health and disease, the good condition and weakness, of that will bring about in the limb those things which the muscle was said to do. And likewise, if the pneuma too is the first of the things that move the leg, these things will be said of it. Come then, for the sake of clarity let these things be laid down by us: that the muscle is moved by the pneuma that is carried through the nerves, and by the muscle first the shin, into which the muscle is inserted, and then through that the articulation at the knee, upon which the whole leg is attached.

For on these assumptions one could truly say both that the muscle itself becomes a weight for the weak pneuma, and together with it the whole limb, for instance, as it [535] may happen, the shin; but if we were to suppose that the nerve is moved by the pneuma, and the muscle by the nerve, and then in turn the shin by the muscle, the weak pneuma will be weighed down by all the things mentioned. So that here too it is already clear that it is not possible to distinguish what primarily weighs down and what is weighed down without having first come to know what primarily moves each of the parts in us. But this too we shall examine more precisely on another occasion; let the matter which the discussion was about be brought to its conclusion. For the sake of clarity the whole exposition will proceed on the basis of an assumption. Let it be supposed, then, that the muscle is what primarily moves both itself and the bone of the shin.

To itself, then, it is never heavy, not even when it is in its most atonic state; but the lower leg weighs upon it. Whether, however, it does so only when the muscle desires to move, or even when it is at rest, would be (ᾖ) a matter for another inquiry, and no small one, which has been determined by us in the writings On the Movement of Muscles; without this inquiry it is not possible to diagnose accurately either the disposition or the affected part on the basis of the sensations of heaviness.
