For instance, in some people either one limb or even [536] the whole body is weighed down when they have resolved to move, whereas when they are at rest no sensation of heaviness arises; others, however, say that they are weighed down even before moving. What, then, the disposition is in each of these two cases it is impossible to know before one has discovered the bodies that move and the bodies that are moved throughout the whole leg. For if the fibres of the nerves in the muscle are the first things moved, and there is moved together with them within it the membranous kind and the venous and the arterial, and further the ligaments, a sensation of heaviness will arise for it both on account of these and on account of all the other things throughout the whole limb; and we shall examine and determine when the heaviness will be present while the limb is acting and moving, and when while it is at rest. But if the class of ligaments in it also moves together with the fleshy part — for these constitute the proper substance of the muscle — then on account of none of these would the sensation of heaviness ever arise; it will arise, rather, either from the veins, or from the arteries, or from the fat, or from the bones, or from some of these, or from all.

It is clear, however, that even if at some point in such divisions we omit the 'from some' or 'from all', those reading the book must supply it in thought, knowing that in all arguments of this kind the conjunctions are not disjunctive but subdisjunctive (paradisjunctive). From what has been said, then, it is quite evident that whoever wishes to be capable of diagnosing a plethoric part must necessarily possess scientific knowledge of the faculties that govern us, and of the anatomy and nature of all the parts of the animal precisely; for setting out from this he might perhaps one day discover signs of a plethoric part. But if someone has no concern for truth, but wishes to deceive his neighbours into thinking that he has come to know something clever, it is ready to hand for him, if nothing else, at least to learn the statements of Erasistratus in the first book of his Hygienic Matters; for in no other work did he even attempt to state signs of plethos. Let us attend, therefore, to his words, first those in which he says what exactly the genesis of plethora is—for so he himself names the plethos in the veins—and then next those in which he sets out the signs of its diagnosis. His account of its genesis, at any rate, is as follows.

For when the nourishment that is being distributed is neither concocted down nor worked off [538] in the manner customary for each person, nor excreted in some other way, it is necessary (ἀναγκαῖον ἦ) that the vessels be filled, since concoction and distribution (and) continue to render the activities that belong to them. And since the nourishment already present in the vessels is in no way consumed, while that coming from the foods taken in is added to it, the vessels in the body are distended still further. And when the vessels no longer admit any further packing-in, and other nourishment is brought up from the belly, what is already present takes an impulse towards the adjacent vessels of the pneuma. From this, then, it is clear that he is discussing the plethos in respect of the filling (ἔγχυμα), and also from his calling it specifically plethora; for only this affection is named plethora, not the other one, which is judged with reference to the faculty. And after going on a little, concerning the diagnosis of it he writes the following: One must therefore, as has been said, try to diagnose the condition that consists in plethora.

At the beginning of it, then, when the vessels are moderately filled, people appear better-toned and stronger than themselves, beyond what is customary; but as they come to a greater degree of filling, the upper arms, the shins and the hands become filled out, [539] as in those who come to a state of distension from exercises; and when the plethora advances far, these parts are sore, slower and harder to move, and the whole body is tense to the touch, since a lassitude (kopos) appears. Such a condition is by now near to disease, unless one resolves it very skilfully and intelligently. In these words Erasistratus has confused the signs of plethoras of different kinds, in addition to ascribing to them some things that are not necessary. One may examine his account from the beginning. For in the statement, 'At the beginning of it, then, when the vessels are moderately filled, people appear better-toned and stronger than themselves, beyond what is customary', the argument has a necessary consequence in neither direction, neither from the condition to its signs, nor from the signs to the condition. For it is neither necessary, when the vessels are moderately filled, that people appear better-toned and stronger than themselves, nor, when they appear such, have the vessels been moderately filled.

For with moderate fillings of these it is possible sometimes for some persons even [540] to become weaker in tone, or to change in no evident way in either direction, neither towards strength nor towards weakness; and if they become stronger than before, it is possible that in them the quantity of the humours has not only increased together with the faculty, but also has at times diminished, and sometimes preserves its original amount. For on either hypothesis it is possible for the first-mentioned item to have a consequence of three things: for the humours' having increased, good tone and lack of tone relative to the previous condition, and further the faculty's remaining within the same limits; and for having become better in tone, both the humours' having increased and their having diminished, and their being in due proportion. And let it be understood in the same way in the present discussion, whether I say 'humours' or 'blood'; for a distinction concerning them will be drawn as the discussion proceeds. Erasistratus, then, made his pronouncement baldly, appending no demonstration to what he said; we, however, not baldly, but confirming each of the things we said just now with necessary demonstrations, shall here too again make our beginning from the very words of Erasistratus: 'they appear', he says, 'better in tone and stronger'.

[541] Does 'better-toned' signify something other than 'stronger', and did he teach us two signs of a moderate plethos, or, though he said two names, did he teach one sign? For my part I find no difference in what is signified, neither in respect of genus nor in respect of species nor in the more and the less, but I consider the same thing to be signified by each of the two. But if you wish, posit that the one indicates an intensification and increase in comparison with the other, whether 'stronger' in comparison with 'better-toned' or 'better-toned' in comparison with 'stronger'; yet what is signified from both is at all events of the same species. And where there is increase, the species remaining the same, there there is no teaching of two things signified. It is quite clear, moreover, that the other genus of plethos, that which is relative to the faculty, Erasistratus does not mention at all, neither in this book nor in the books On Fevers.

For plethora, according to him, is the cause of paremptosis, upon which inflammations are formed and fever follows; and the generation of plethora he showed clearly in the passage quoted above, in which he says that the vessels in the body are crammed full and distended to the greatest extent [542]. For he himself used these very expressions, just as he also said that, because they are no longer able to receive the cramming, a paremptosis of the surplus into the arteries takes place, the matters abounding in the veins having taken their impulse thither. Something, then, has been left out here too in the division. For he ought not to have said thus simply that, when the veins no longer admit cramming, the impulse of their contents is toward the vessels of the pneuma; it would have been far better to say that one of two things follows upon the aforesaid filling of the veins, either a rupture of the tunic itself or a transfusion of the blood into the vessels of the pneuma. But to suppose that the blood is of necessity transfused because it is not contained by the veins is the mark of one who has altogether forgotten that rupture of a vessel sometimes occurs through plethos—to pass over the anastomosis without transfusion that manifestly often takes place into perceptible open spaces, those of the intestines and the belly and the stomachos and the pharynx and the mouth.

But deficiency in the division of the arguments [543] is habitual with Erasistratus not only in this case but also in nearly all his other treatises. Let us, then, examine once more what has been said, whatever it may amount to. "When the vessels are moderately filled, people appear more vigorous than they were." Is this so, Erasistratus, even if the strength of the body is not increased together with the quantity of the blood, or only when it too is increased along with it? For I, for my part, say that it is most necessary, for the vigour of the activity, that the strength of the faculty also be increased. And so, if you think that the activities of the faculty become stronger by the increase of the blood alone, you would seem to overturn the faculties even more than Asclepiades does. For not even he says simply thus, that whoever has more blood is in every case more vigorous, and whoever has less is of necessity less vigorous; rather, you will find that he states certain distinctions which agree with the phenomena, even though he holds that there is no faculty in us at all, neither psychic nor vital.

For some people are seen at times to have become both more full of blood than they themselves were and at the same time stronger, [544] others stronger and at the same time poorer in blood; so that necessarily, since strength is neither increased by the abundance of blood nor diminished by its reduction, one must consider that these things too were stated rather carelessly by Erasistratus. For if someone had reminded him of what I have now gone through, he would not have denied that the vigour of the activities follows not upon an increase of blood but upon the strength of the faculty. Let us then ourselves now make his statement more complete, adding what is lacking to what he said deficiently. It will be as follows: when the blood increases together with the faculty, the vigour too must necessarily increase. And yet, even if we were to say this, we shall be saying something true, but we gain nothing further for the matters at hand from this either.

For the statement that, in those in whom both have increased together, the blood and the faculty, vigour too has increased, will be truly said; but the statement that, in those in whom strength has increased, both have of necessity increased, is false. For the faculty does not of necessity increase together with the blood when it has been increased, but it is possible that sometimes the faculty alone [increases]. [545] At any rate the truly good trainer, if he were to take over someone who through lack of exercise has accumulated much phlegmatic blood but is rather weak in faculty, will in a short time render this man stronger, not more full of blood, than he received him. Just as, then, it is not necessary that those who have become more vigorous than themselves in their activities should have had their humours increased, so it is necessary that those who have become more vigorous than themselves in their activities should have had their faculty become stronger. And not only when you begin from vigour will you of necessity follow on to the robustness of the faculty, but also from the faculty to vigour; for he who is strong in faculty is more vigorous in his activities. So that they reciprocally follow one another: vigour in the activities follows robustness of faculty, and robustness in the faculty follows vigour of the activities; for whichever of them you should suppose to be present, the other too in every case is present together with it. From the greater quantity of blood, however, the consequence is not necessary.

For neither, if this is greater than before, is the man of necessity more vigorous, nor, if it is less, less vigorous, just as neither, when it is equal, is he in a similar condition with respect to power. [546] So that it is clear from what has been said that the vigour of the activities is a sign at once proper and inseparable of the power's being strong, but of the increase of the blood it is neither proper nor inseparable. But what Erasistratus said next is not a proper sign of plethora, though it is an inseparable one. He names it 'being filled up' (παρεμπίμπλασθαι), but it would more clearly be named 'being stretched' (τείνεσθαι). And indeed the more precise of the gymnastic trainers too, when they call one of the fatigues ulcerous, another tensive, and another inflammatory, indicate nothing other than that the limbs are filled up in the case of the tensive fatigue. For they say that any part whatsoever of themselves has been filled up at the moment when they perceive some tension in it. Now they perceive tension also in inflammation, but with that there is present, either always or for the most part, the pulsation contrary to nature, which someone expressing it more vividly will call throbbing pain; but in those to whom nothing else has happened besides being stretched, in these the part that is stretched is neither inflamed nor is it of necessity plethoric, but one of two things, either fatigued or plethoric.

But if [547] it is fatigue-like, it was affected in this way following rather many exertions; and if the person did not exert himself at all, the part does not become fatigue-like because of fatigue, but in some other way. So that it is true to say that, since there is a sensation of tension without one's having exercised, there is in every case plethora. And, when we put it in this way, the sign becomes at once both inseparable and proper, since each of the two necessarily follows upon the other: for tension without exercises follows upon plethora, since it becomes an inseparable sign of it, as being brought about by plethora as its cause; whereas an increase of the blood to such a degree as not yet to distend the veins is not yet plethora. Why ever, then, did Erasistratus make mention in his account of upper arms and shanks and hands? For such tension arises also in the neck and the back and the loins and in the thorax and in the hypogastrium.

But just as Erasistratus mentioned the limbs superfluously, in the same way, and even more so, he also mentioned the ulcerous sensation; for this is not a sign of plethora, but arises upon biting humours, of the kind that arises in ulcerated parts, either when something touches them, or when an ichor irritates them, [548] or when a drug bites them, or even arises in movements alone. For just as tension is proper to a plethos of humours distending the containing vessels, so the ulcerous sensation follows upon a biting quality; and for this reason it is sometimes present in many people even throughout the whole body, not merely when they have no plethora, but when they do not even have the commensurate amount of blood. And if these things are so, as indeed they are, it is now time to make a determination concerning one of the matters which we deferred earlier, since up to this point we were examining the signs written down by Erasistratus. For as regards plethos, whether it be conceived in relation to the faculty or in relation to the space of the containing vessels, it would surely have been better to determine whether it is of a nature to arise in blood alone, or also in all the other humours; but this too has been left undetermined by them.

Since, then, not only these affections, deficiency and plethora, befall the humours, but also an abnormal quality, I asked all the physicians, both those who understand plethora relative to the faculty and those who understand it relative to the increase of the fluids, whether, [549] when the blood alone has been increased to such a degree as not to be contained, it will come about that the veins are stretched; but if either phlegm, into any other part whatsoever, or into the veins themselves, or, together with this or apart from this, some bile, or ichor, or flatulent pneuma should be gathered into so great a quantity as to be no longer held by what contains it, will it not in this case too be necessary that the animal perceive tension? If the part that is being stretched is capable of sensation, it is necessary, in the case of everything that distends and is not contained, that the perception of tension arise in the animal, and that the affection itself, the so-called tension, befall the parts; and when this increases further, the thing being stretched must also burst. To me, at any rate, such a view seems to agree with what is evidently observed. For not only sinews or ropes are seen bursting from the violence of the tension, but often also wine-jars, from must that has turned to pneuma.

Recently, at any rate, a tin vessel was so greatly inflated by the drug contained in it, the one prepared from vipers, that both the leather wrapped around it and the cord with which it had been tied burst, and [550] the lid was bulged outward. And indeed that some people are at times seized by the greatest pains when flatulent pneuma has been trapped in certain parts of the animal, and that this is wont to happen especially in the colon, I think is known to all who take care to follow and examine what is seen every day in the case of the sick. It is better, therefore, to hold that the parts are brought into a tensive condition by every moist and pneumatic substance, than that such an affection follows upon blood alone among the humours when it increases in quantity. Let us pass again, then, to those who think that plethora is always constituted in relation to the faculty, and let us ask these too one of the most obvious questions, positing some such hypothesis as the following, by way of example.

(parts) Let two men carry burdens, having set them upon their shoulders, the one a piece of wood, or a stone, or some very heavy load, the other a very few, very sharp thorns; then, in the face of such a spectacle, let us ask those who always conceive of plethora in relation to the faculty whether they also call the few thorns a load, or whether being distressed by each of the things carried [551] is a symptom common to the two men, while the form of the distress differs very greatly: for to the one it has happened to be weighed down without being pricked, to the other to be pricked without being weighed down. And in general, if someone calls being pricked, or bitten, or being distressed in any way whatsoever a load and a plethora, he will at some point be compelled to call even a single thorn or a very fine needle a load—than which what could be more ridiculous? These things, then, are absurd and contrary to the common notions of all men. But it is our purpose not to overturn but to preserve the common notions. We hold, then, that what weighs down is 'much', whereas what bites, or pricks, or however one may wish to name it, is 'distressing'. And indeed that many of the humors are biting, some having their generation in ourselves, others being brought to us from outside, this is evident to everyone.

There are four differences among them in respect of the more and the less: for those that bite moderately are itch-producing, like squill; those that bite more vehemently are biting, like the onion—for if our body should be in contact for a longer time with such a nature of body, it will be ulcerated; [552] and those that are still more pungent than this, and especially when they are applied to ulcerated parts, produce shivering. And when the shivering has been extended and increased, the symptom is named rigor. By the same analogy there arise in us biting humours according to four forms: for of these, those that scratch moderately are itch-producing; those more biting than these produce an ulcerous sensation; those biting more than these, shivering; and those sufficiently biting, rigor. These matters have been discussed in many treatises, but for one who wishes to obtain some synopsis of them, what has been said in the second book of On the Causes in the Symptoms and in the fourth of the Hygiene is sufficient; and if one were also to read through the work On the Power of Drugs and the treatise that precedes these, the one On Mixtures, he would in this way be persuaded more scientifically about the nature of biting things.

But the majority of physicians have suffered something similar to what was said by Hippocrates concerning those who, in the case of fractures or some such affections, do not do what is prescribed; for those too, although they wish to become healthy, [553] do not endure the toil involved in the treatment, just as these do not endure the toil involved in learning. But it is not possible either for the former to become healthy all at once, attaining the end by the mere wishing, or for the latter to become scientific without traversing the whole road which I have just now set out. For they will come to know, if they should wish it, that the ulcerous sensation of the whole body, both that which arises upon more numerous exercises undertaken contrary to habit and that which forms suddenly without exercises, is the offspring of a biting humour. And for this reason the gymnastic trainers treat those who have exercised too much with more abundant oil and soft rubbing and warm baths of sweet waters that are precisely well-tempered, so that the biting humours may be dispersed—all those that were generated, when they exercised rather immoderately, upon the colliquation of fat and of soft flesh, or on account of the humours in the body themselves having been strongly heated.

If, then, someone should endure to learn thoroughly the demonstrations of these matters, he alone would be firmly persuaded that the ulcerous condition arises in consequence of biting humours, the condition of heaviness in consequence of humours that are many in relation to the faculty, and the condition of tension in consequence of humours that are many, this one too, but [554] in relation to the space that contains them, not to the faculty of the (contained) bodies. Erasistratus, in the first book of his Hygieina, when going through the very genesis of plethora, teaches most clearly the third of the conditions mentioned; but when he next turns to the signs, he has written no more the signs of this condition than those of the others. For tension belongs to this one alone—what he named paremimplasthai (being filled up alongside); but the sensation's becoming ulcerous is the proper sign neither of the aforesaid plethos nor of the plethos in relation to the faculty; and still less is their being rendered heavier and harder to move; for this too is proper to the plethos in relation to the faculty.

So he very nearly wrote out for us the whole syndrome of the Empiricists; indeed, he even wrote a part of the so-called three-time semeiosis, which the followers of Herophilus introduced in the same way as the Empiricists, when he spoke thus: 'for when the nutriment that is being distributed is neither fully concocted nor worked off by exertion according to what is customary for each person, nor in some other way excreted' — for it makes no difference whether one says these things or, as they put it, [555] 'an idle life and retention of the habitual excretions.' For he indicated the preceding idle life by saying 'nor worked off by exertion according to what is customary for each,' and the retention of the excretions by adding 'nor otherwise excreted,' (the semeiosis of plethos by means of time) taking from the time that has gone before the idle life together with the retention of the excretions; from the now present time the being filled up and the ulcerous condition, reluctance toward movements, and heaviness of the whole body, and whatever other such things they add; and from the future, that those in such a state, once evacuated, have been well benefited — which has been left out by Erasistratus. For this is a testimony to the correct diagnosis and at the same time to the treatment; but it would be no part of diagnosis — or, as they call it, semeiosis — if indeed it is through semeiosis that we wish to infer the conditions from signs, in order that we may discover the appropriate treatment. So that if it were possible, setting out from something else, to treat appropriately, the semeiosis would be superfluous.

And in making mention of the present time, he has omitted redness and distension of the vessels, [556] which almost all the empiricists, and not a few of the dogmatists, also add, just as they add certain other things, as has been said. And yet, for those who posit that the genesis of plethora occurs in blood alone, it is not wrongly that redness and the distension of the vessels are added to the diagnosis in their case; and still more so, since he will set down the statement that the upper arms and hands and lower legs are filled up as a sign no more of the plethos in the flesh and the whole muscles than of that of the veins, following his own hypotheses. But even so it was in any case necessary to make a twofold diagnosis, one of the plethos of these perceptible veins, which all of us human beings see, and the other of that which he alone beheld. I think, then, that it has by now become plain, to those at least who pay attention, that it is no small matter to diagnose plethos. And where it is not easy to diagnose it even at the level of argument, but it is in every way perplexing, scarcely indeed could it be set right in actual practice by mere chance by those who have neither examined anything beforehand concerning it nor discovered anything.

[557] Let us, then, begin the discussion of plethos once more from the Empiricists, since they seem to escape quite safely from the aporiai that have been mentioned, by admitting that they themselves know nothing at all about the substance of plethos, while asserting that in the case of a certain syndrome of the following kind the removal of blood has been observed to be beneficial—a syndrome which they call plethoric. For, having gathered together into one everything that has been stated by each of the Dogmatists, they suppose that on this basis they escape the aporiai of those men, yet they are refuted far more seriously than they, if one attends carefully to what they say—all of which it is better to go through again from the beginning.

Let it be supposed, then, that in the preceding time the regimen was the customary one with respect to the foods used from the beginning, and in some of them in greater repletion than before, with a retention of the excretion, and the whole manner of life idle; while in the present there is tension of the whole body, or of certain parts, sluggishness toward movements, weakness in the activities, and a sensation of heaviness and of an ulcerous condition, together with the swelling of the veins; and let there be added, if you wish, the redness too, since this too [558] is stated by some, and indeed also the bulk of the whole body, and a certain uneven and fatigue-like condition; for there are those who add these as well. We shall ask them, then, what I myself, when I was a youth, asked my Empiricist teacher when he first taught me these things: whether all the things mentioned must come together at once for what they themselves call the recollection of the evacuation, or whether, even if they see one of them, they will phlebotomize at once? To the first question, then, he readily answered me, saying that all must come together; for the syndrome is a thing of such a kind, a collection of all the items that make it complete.

But when I first reminded him of two men whom that very man had recently ordered to be phlebotomized—the one suffering severely from ophthalmia, the other having fallen from a carriage and then become entangled in the reins and dragged for a considerable distance, so that certain parts were bruised—and when, after this, he kept silent, I recalled yet another man, whom he also phlebotomized although he had only a moderate fever but could not bear the pain of his head; and another, a pleuritic, [559] this one too not having the whole aforementioned syndrome; he was reduced to the greatest perplexity. And so I went on at greater length to recount to him certain other similar cases as well, but I also reminded him concerning those already mentioned, that he had phlebotomized them when they were so far from having the whole syndrome that I, for my part, said I could not recall even any two of these signs being present in the men. For the man who fell from the carriage—one who exercised every day, and was sufficiently evacuated by all the customary excretions, and ate in due measure, and spent nearly the whole day in our company, and seemed neither to him nor to anyone else to need evacuation—when, having been thrown down, he had certain parts bruised, he judged him in need of phlebotomy, though he had acquired neither any redness, nor swelling of the vessels, nor anything else from the signs of the syndrome, but only had pain in the bruised parts.

In the same way too the man with ophthalmia and the man suffering pain in the head, who had none at all of the things mentioned in the plethoric syndrome; and I know of many others besides who were venesected by us, either having nothing at all from the plethoric syndrome, [560] or at any rate not all together of the things stated by us. For now, I said, as I recall to myself those whom I have seen venesected by you, I can find none among them who had the whole syndrome consisting in such symptoms; but one was venesected because he was in a state of lassitude, having nothing else; another because he was fevering violently, or suffering pain in the eyes, or the head, or had his haemorrhoids suppressed, or, in the case of a woman, her menses, but not all the things which the plethoric syndrome requires to come together. If, then, you call plethoric all the conditions in which venesection has been observed to be beneficial, it is time for us to call ophthalmia, pleurisy, violent pain, a fall from a carriage, and countless other things plethoric syndromes; but if none of these is contained in the plethoric syndrome, and it is the aggregate of the symptoms previously mentioned that is named the plethoric syndrome, then one must venesect no one before he has all of them.

How, then, that man met me in reply to these points, and gave no fitting answer, is a task for long leisure, [561] not a task proper to what now lies before us; but I, since I have at present no leisure for idle talk, have decided not now, but in the discourse on phlebotomy — there I have chosen to set forth all the indications of the remedy, which not even themselves has anyone written down precisely and with proper distinctions. Leaving aside, then, for the present the argument against the Empiricists, I return again to the Rationalists, examining each of the symptoms which they wrote down. For some of them belong to the plethora relative to the faculty, some to the plethora according to the filling (ἔγχυμα); some are not simply signs of plethora, but of a plethora of such-and-such a kind; and some are signs of no plethora at all, but either of cacochymia and corruption, or of a weak faculty, or of bulk of the solid bodies. That this is so, you would learn if you applied your mind to what is about to be said.

The tensive condition, then, whenever it occurs without exercises, indicates in every case that a large quantity of substance is contained in a sentient body; it does not, however, further indicate what the substance is, or its kind—at least in respect of this alone, namely the being stretched itself, which is common [562] to every substance, thin, thick, and intermediate in consistency, and pneumatic, and further hot and cold, or intermediate—but it requires certain other distinguishing signs for the determination of this. The atony in the activities, on the other hand, shows the faculty to be weaker, in that the mover is checked, as in the case of a weak movement of the hands; for it follows upon many states. For whether the fleshy and the fatty kind have been increased in someone, while the faculty remains within the same limits, it is necessary that the movements become more lacking in tone, since the mover remains equal while the moved has been increased; or whether some one of the humours, or indeed all together, are in excess, the faculty not having been increased along with them, in this case too it is necessary that the activities become more lacking in tone; or whether both have been increased together, both what are called the parenchymata and the fluids, but the faculty has not been increased along with them; or whether, these remaining as they were, the faculty has become weaker.

And it could sometimes happen that both come together, so that the faculty becomes weaker [563] and the humours together with the parenchymata are either more or fewer—either one of these two, whichever it may be; and on account of these things too the activities become weaker, each of them occurring singly, or two together, or more, or all at once. For to suppose that a weaker motion could ever be produced as a result of the good nourishment of the solid bodies belongs to men who do not recognise that the faculties extend through the whole of the solid bodies, but who set up the arteries and the nerves as pipes or conduits for pneuma. You will learn the faultiness of this opinion from many other sources, but not least also from two of our treatises, that On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato and that On the Natural Faculties. Now the good nourishment of the solid bodies is what is proper to good condition (euexia), whereas the increase of the fleshes is proper to good-fleshedness (eusarkia) and much-fleshedness (polysarkia). For the most part, then, the fat increases more, in proportion; but sometimes the flesh increases more within fat (ἐν πιμελῇ), or fat alone. These matters have been discussed in the commentaries On Mixtures.

And just as in the case of flesh there is on the one hand good-fleshedness (eusarkia), on the other much-fleshedness (polysarkia), [564] in the same way in the case of blood there is on the one hand what is, as it were, a kind of good-bloodedness (euaimia), and on the other much-bloodedness (polyaimia). Now the condition of good-bloodedness is clearly, in both quality and quantity, exactly according to nature; whereas that of much-bloodedness is blameless in respect of quality, but in respect of quantity not blameless, but in every case more, either than what exists according to nature from birth, or than what is in proportion to the faculty. For it is possible at times for both to increase together with one another beyond the nature from birth, both the strength of the faculty and the quantity of blood, as in the athletic good conditions (euexiai); for indeed the moist and the fleshy parts and the faculty increase together in proportion to one another in them. And so it is now evident that those who have declared the bulk of the body to be one of the plethoric signs do not speak the truth either; for bulk of the veins would be a plethoric sign, but bulk of flesh and fat would be a plethora of those very things, not however that which we are now investigating, which is indeed also called plethora.

For having set out to speak about this plethos, which evidently indicates evacuation, some among them went astray to such an extent—a thing which homonymies at times bring about (ὅ ποτε ὁμωνυμίαις ἐνδείκνυται)—[565] as to be carried off to the plethos of flesh and of fat. Thus, then, bulk of the body is a bad sign of plethos; for it would be indicative of the filling of those veins themselves which we see, but not necessarily of those in the depth; rather, it is possible at times, even when the outer veins are distended, that the inner ones are not distended in the same way; for example, straightaway when cold takes hold, the blood is driven into the depth, and the outer veins are so drained of blood as not even to be visible; and again, when warmth arises, or when people have bathed, the blood is carried to the skin and the outer parts of the body, abandoning the depth; and if there should also be a burning fever, it is necessary then too that the blood be burnt in the body, as though it were boiling, and be turned into pneuma and diffused. So that bulk of the veins is not an inseparable sign of a plethos of humours; rather, first there must be such a condition in the body that neither the inner parts exceed the outer nor the latter the former in heat; and second, that there not be immoderate heat throughout the whole animal.

[566] Once these things have been determined in advance, the swelling of the veins might on occasion be a sign of the sanguineous plethora now under discussion, that which is such by predominance; for it is impossible that blood so exact should ever be contained in the veins that nothing either of bile, or of phlegm, or of serous ichor is carried along in it, which is why in what preceded too I asked that it be understood in the same way, whether I should say that the humours are in excess or the blood. For since blood unmixed and pure of the other fluids is never contained in the veins—for this has been shown by us elsewhere—but rather blood that is mixed, not however at random, but with the others mixed into it in a certain due proportion in animals that are in their natural state, it will make no difference whether one calls it humours or blood.

For when all of them increase together, in their natural proportion, along with the blood which prevails by predominance, the name 'humours' signifies the same thing, and it makes no difference whether one says that the humours have increased or the blood, since the statement that speaks of 'the humours' shows precisely this, that the excess has come about entirely in keeping with the original proportion. Let this, then, be so determined by us, and let us return once more to [567] the matter before us. For the swelling of the veins, if it has come about neither through the predominance of the external condition nor through diffusion and boiling, indicates that the plethora is sanguineous.

And such a part must neither have been positioned in a downward-sloping posture, nor have been recently moved more than the others. Hence, too, one who embraced all the particular distinctions in a single formula would say that the swelling of the veins indicates a plethora of blood when all the parts have the same condition together with a well-proportioned heat; since if all were disposed alike, but the heat were immoderate, in this case there occurs a diffusion of the humours which raises the veins into swelling, and yet it indicates not a sanguineous plethora but a pneumatic one; for the humours are turned into pneuma when heated. Hence also those who declared that the swelling of the veins signifies plethora will seem to have spoken correctly, provided one supplies in addition in the statement 'in those veins in which this happens to be occurring'; for the substance that has produced the swelling in the veins is necessarily greater than before; yet it is not yet at all clear what sort of thing the plethora [568] is; for the swelling contrary to nature is common to every abundant substance, whether it be pure blood, or bilious, or serous, or phlegmatic, or pneumatic. And just as this is common to every variety of plethora, so too is the stretching of the veins; for this too follows upon the quantity of the plethora, not upon the difference in kind. Consequently the swelling and the tensive sensation will indicate a plethora of humours no more than one of pneuma. If, then, someone were to declare in some such way as this, 'in the case of tensive sensations there is necessarily plethora', he will speak the truth; and indeed even if he were to say thus, 'plethora in sensitive parts brings on a certain disposition', he too will speak the truth; but if someone, abandoning the generic name 'plethora' or 'humours', were to take 'blood' into the statement, he will not necessarily speak the truth, for the reasons we have stated. And that there is a difference, in the swellings of the veins and in the tensive disposition, not of plethora simply, but of the more and the less in it, is clear from the following.

No part suffers pain when it is being filled, without a violent tension having first come about in it; [569] but if it is raised into a swelling, yet not yet violently, it is not yet stretched. Hence, among swellings, the one accompanied by tension will indicate a greater plethora, the one without it, a lesser. How then is it that sometimes no swelling at all appears in the veins, while the tensive sensation is strong? For surely the condition of being stretched ought to be yoked to the greatest swellings. Either it is because there are times when the swelling distends only the veins in the depth, or, if indeed the plethora about which we are now discoursing belongs among things relative to something—both that relative to the width of the vessels, which we in fact call plethora, when they are not yet being stretched, and that relative to the tension of the coat—then clearly the genesis of the swelling of the veins advances as the blood increases into plethora beyond the natural due proportion of each, so that 'much' is said relative to that; whereas the coat's being stretched indicates (διὰ) an excess over the due proportion relative to the coat itself. For it is not in accordance with nature that this too should be stretched. Each, then, is 'much': both the blood relative to the natural due proportion and that relative to the tension of the coat.

Erasistratus made mention of both, [570] not in an articulated way, nor so clearly as I do now, yet in such a way as to make plain that the nature of the matter is twofold. For in saying, "At the beginning, then, and when the vessels are moderately filled, they appear more well-toned and stronger than their usual selves, beyond what is customary," he indicated the disproportion of the blood beyond what is according to nature for each individual; but in what he adds next, saying, "but when they come to a greater degree of filling, the upper arms and hands and shins become filled out," he indicated that disproportion which is relative to the coats that contain the blood; so that there are two limits of the increase of the blood beyond what is according to nature: one consisting in the coats of the veins being filled, raised into a swelling beyond what is according to nature for each individual; the other, in which, in addition to this, it comes about that they are stretched—neither of these being seen in the plethora relative to the faculty. On these matters, then, this too is sufficient. Redness, which they also mention, is a sign not of plethora simply, but of sanguineous plethora.

And it too will require the same distinctions as the swelling does; [571] for if it is due to some external cause, such as sun, or a bath, or exercise, or a walk, or, to put it simply, heat—and likewise also anger, shame and all such things; and acute fevers too are of this class. So when the condition of the whole body is uniform, and none of the things I have mentioned is present, then the redness would be a sign of sanguineous fullness throughout the whole animal; but if not, then at least in that part in which it appears. For such a colour also accompanies inflammations, whether they form in the muscles or in the skins, since they are plethoric diseases. But concerning inflammations enough has been said in another book, in which we investigated swellings contrary to nature, showing that all of them are formed by a fullness of humours descending now upon one part, now upon another; but now the discussion is not about these, but, as was said before, about that fullness which is called plethora, when an excess of humours forms in the whole body.

But we do not say that plethos is constituted in the whole body [572] in such a way that both kinds of bodies have been harmed, both that of the vessels and that of the fleshes; for it is possible sometimes for only one of the two to be so, as would be the case if whichever part were seized, this happening not in some one part or two, but either throughout the whole animal or in the most numerous and the most principal parts. And so, to discover what sort of thing the bulk is requires a man sufficiently exercised in diagnoses. In the fleshy kind, at any rate, one bulk is that of the fleshes themselves, another that of the humours, the flesh being filled, like some wool or a sponge, with superfluous moisture; but such a plethos in the fleshes is analogous to that in the vessels which is called plethos in respect of the filling, while the other plethos is analogous to that in relation to the faculty, or with heaviness—we bearing in mind that it makes no difference whether one discourses about composite flesh or about muscles, and that if ever the discussion should come to be about the plethos in the fleshes, one must understand the muscles, not that simple flesh which is named by some parenchyma.

In the arteries and the veins, however, the plethora relative to the faculty is not [573] similarly perceptible to the patients themselves; rather, only in those who are by nature most sensitive does a certain faint and deep-seated heaviness make itself apparent throughout the body. Therefore one must seek certain other, clearer indications of such plethora. But since most physicians have been negligent about this matter, some not having investigated it at all and some only deficiently, no more secure indication has been found than the motion of the arteries, which we have expounded sufficiently in the treatises on the pulses. For in most cases the veins come into a state of plethora together with the arteries, on account of the confluence of the vessels, which we have often demonstrated elsewhere; but sometimes, when viscous or thick humours have accumulated in the veins, their transfer into the arteries does not come about easily — though such a case is rare; for unless the humours are extremely thick or viscous, they will in any case flow across.

In such conditions, then, no clear sign of the plethos gathered in the veins can be obtained from the movement of the arteries, however much Nicarchus and Praxagoras may think so, even though they do not grant [574] the arteries any share of blood. In the other conditions of plethora, however, one must trust the signs drawn from the pulses, which have been set out in their proper treatise, and distinguish the forms of plethos, at least when it is evenly extended throughout the whole body, in the following way. For the plethos of blood is deep red, that of yellow bile somewhat pale-yellow; and the colour turns toward whiter than the natural when phlegm predominates, just as toward darker if black bile does. In each of the cases mentioned the blood too must have increased along with it; for if the bile called pale-yellow and yellow should ever be in excess by itself, as in icteric patients, such an affection is no longer plethos, nor a plethoric condition, but cacochymia. The same holds also in the case of black bile and phlegm. But when, as was said earlier, there is either heaviness or bulk beyond what is natural, such a condition has been called plethoric, and from the colour one must recognise the form of the predominant humour.

Bile alone can produce neither of the inseparable symptoms of plethora [575] — neither, then, the swelling nor the heaviness; for some other affection will arise from it before it is increased to so great a degree. Only phlegm, if indeed anything, and this not every phlegm simply, but that found in the dropsies called leucophlegmatic, will be able to abound in the whole body. And it is clear that the humour called crude also must, in the present discussion at least, be set down as one of the kinds of phlegm; since if we posit it as something distinct from that, it is necessary to add, to the differentiae of plethora which we mentioned just now, also the one arising from such a humour. This humour is thicker than the other phlegm and less pneumatic, such as settles in the urines, especially in those of people who, from gluttony, have a copious sediment resembling bean-soup; and indeed such a humour has often passed downward all at once in those bodies which abstained from exercises but made use of very many foods, and of baths after meals; but with this humour too, just as with phlegm, a certain white pallor coexists throughout the whole body.

As for the other kinds of phlegm, one [576] is sweet, another sour, another salty; and people become somnolent when the sweet kind is in excess, hungry when the sour kind is in excess, just as they become thirsty when the salty kind prevails; and they become without appetite with the aforementioned raw humour. As regards sleep, in the case of the other phlegms mentioned above it is a little more than what is in accordance with nature; but the raw humour, like the sweet phlegm, clearly renders people somnolent. For it has been shown elsewhere that when the sensory principle is moistened and cooled, the comatose condition follows, just as sleeplessness also follows when it is dried and heated. For this reason, then, those who suffer from bile are all sleepless, with either of the two biles; and in the case of the black bile there is present in addition, as a distinctive feature, sullenness and despondency without reason. But if the aforementioned humours should not be in excess throughout the whole body, but be gathered together in some one part, they produce swellings contrary to nature in those very bodies, concerning which demonstration is given elsewhere.

And the very symptoms of them that have now been mentioned, apart from the bad colour, belong to them when they have occupied the brain and the stomachos [577]; for sleeplessness and sleep come about on account of the brain, while appetites and losses of appetite come about on account of the stomachos, which is disposed differently at different times. And it is clear that the mouth of the stomach has here been called stomachos, in which the phlegm that has gathered, as was said a little earlier, produced the appetites; but of the bilious humours, in the case of the yellow they will be thirsty and nauseous, and their mouth is bitter; whereas in the case of the black, they are despondent, sullen, fearful, without thirst, and full of saliva, but not all of them averse to food, only some of them. And those are considerably hungry in whom the black bile has the acid quality predominating; and this comes about when it is rendered more malignant. But so long as it is merely like a sediment of blood, and not yet precisely acid, it is perhaps better (so far as it is called a melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile either, but, as I am accustomed, melancholic, because it has come near to becoming black bile.

But now is not the occasion to go through the difference among the cacochymiai, since I said that they are not even called plethos; for our proposed task was not simply to discover what is in excess in whatever manner, but to inquire about plethos; [578] and this is an excess of the humours throughout the whole body of the animal. One ought not, then, to desire to hear in this discourse about the forms either of the local swellings or of cacochymia, but about when either all the humours are increased according to their original proportion, or one of them acquires some slight preponderance. Now blood can acquire a very great preponderance in the plethoric dispositions, but none of the other humours can; for such a thing is already cacochymia, and is no longer called plethos, nor plethora.

Hence also the pulses in the cacochymias are precisely proper to the nature of the humours; but in the cases of plethos that have been mentioned they do not preserve their differences with equal clarity, because the humour that is in excess is in every case accompanied by abundant blood. But when it prevails strongly, in the case of yellow bile the pulses must necessarily become such as we said follow when the heart is being dried and heated; and in the case of black bile, such in turn as we said arise if it is cooled and dried; and by the same [579] reasoning, if phlegm should ever overcome the others, it will produce pulses that are the offspring of a cold and moist disposition. Upon blood that is precisely in accordance with nature no alteration of the original condition follows; but when moister blood is in excess, the pulses too are altered along with it, just as if it should become hotter or colder than itself. All such matters have been distinguished in the treatise on the pulses; for now it will suffice to say only this much, that from idleness and a moist regimen the blood would become moister than itself, through an excess of the watery residues; and from anger and exercises, from exposures to scorching heat and from rubbings, from a heating drug, from nourishment of that kind, and from wines less diluted and older, hotter; just as also through some recent chilling, colder. And if someone should for a longer time use foods that are drier in their mixture, yet have no other dyskrasia, that blood would become drier.

And indeed also by way of conjunction it will be rendered moister and colder, or colder and drier, hotter and moister, or hotter and drier, in consequence of the aforementioned [580] causes, without any one of the other humours having gained the upper hand. But if it should also arrive at a dyscrasia through the admixture of those humours, such a dyscrasia would be constituted together with cacochymia, the blood being still, even now, said to have become either hotter, or colder and moister, and likewise in the case of the other six dyscrasias—for there were eight in all—but in a different manner, not as when it was such only in and by itself.

The pulses, in accordance with the eight dyscrasias, will have that form which we went through in the treatise on the pulses; and whether, as has been said, it belongs to the blood alone, or is due to some admixture of a humour, one must distinguish by the colour accompanying the whole body and by the other symptoms—as many as have been mentioned a little earlier concerning sleep and wakefulness, or appetite and lack of appetite, or anything else of the kind—and by the regimen that has preceded, and the exercises, and the things that habitually befall the patient himself, and further by the season and the region and the natural density and rarity of the body; for it is better to take the assurance for the diagnosis from all of these, not from one or two, knowing well that this alone in the [581] art has the greatest share in conjecture—I mean this whole diagnostic part of the art, not only that which concerns cacochymia or plethos, which it is now our task to distinguish; for the matters concerning the activities, or the causes of diseases, or the cures, have a knowledge that is more scientific. These very matters have been discussed at greater length elsewhere, and now it will suffice, having adequately determined what has been added, to bring the treatise to a close at just about this point. And the account would become sufficient if examined on an example. Let it be supposed, then, that the man is free of fever, but that his veins are of greater volume and his whole body redder.

One must therefore consider whether none of the heating causes has come near this man; for if it should appear that one has, it is better to postpone the diagnosis until the movement arising from that cause has settled down throughout the whole body, since it is not fitting to bring to diagnosis a man who is angry, or has bathed, or is bathing, or has exercised, or has just taken wine, or has been heated in any other way whatsoever, but one who is at rest from all external movements; for if at that [582] time he should appear of this sort, blood is in excess in the man. From there one should examine the other signs, first those that have the greatest force, then the rest in order; it was shown that heaviness and tension have this, and the reluctance towards movements, then next the matters pertaining to the pulses, wakefulness and sleep, appetites and lack of appetite, and whatever other things are of this kind. After these, each of the antecedent causes that produce plethos: whether some customary excretion has been held back, whether exercise has been neglected, whether foods in greater quantity and highly nourishing have been taken continually, whether he makes use of unaccustomed baths after food, and in addition to these, further, whether such a man is frequently seized by plethoric diseases.

In addition to all these, adding also the factors deriving from the region and the season, or anything else of this kind, not assigning an equal share of causation to all, just as one does not in the other parts of the art either; for some of the signs are scientific, such as tension, heaviness, the swelling of the veins, reluctance, the colour, and the movement of the pulses—all recent movements, of course, having been set aside; but some fall short of these, such as the suppression of the excretions, [583] an idle life, foods more abundant and more nourishing, and baths after food; yet when all of these come together they come close to the scientific ones. Third in rank after these is whether the person is habitually seized by plethoric diseases; and next the factors relating to regions and seasons, which are constitutive of all of them; for in winter and spring, and in cold and temperate regions, people accumulate plethora more, but in hot and dry seasons and regions less; and likewise those who are dense in their surface do so more, while those who are loose-textured do so more rarely.

B.translation: [513] GALEN'S BOOK ON PLETHORA. One cannot find almost all present-day physicians either naming any other name more often than that of plethora, or being more ignorant of anything else than of this. At any rate, of those among them who are able both to give and to receive an account, most answer those who ask what it is that they call plethora that the name is said in the category of the relative (ἐν τῷ πρὸς τί), just as 'much' and 'little' are, so that it is not possible to comprehend it within a measure; for what is much for one thing is sometimes rather little for another.

And when you question them, asking them to state the thing in relation to which they say [514] plethora exists, some become more voiceless than fish, while others babble such long and outlandish nonsense that one cannot follow what they are saying. Very few answer that the much and the little are understood as in relation to the faculty; and if you question them again as to what they mean by faculty, some make no answer at all, and of those who venture to declare something, no one says the same thing as anyone else, and most explain anything rather than a faculty. But if anyone among them should be found sensible enough to say that the faculty is either an active substance or an active cause, and should then be asked, first, whether there is some such substance governing the animal, and then, if there is, to set out what exactly it is, not even this man answers any longer when questioned on the point at issue, but either falls completely silent or carries the discussion off to something such that it would be better to be silent.

But if even among these someone should be found so far sensible as to say that he cannot state what the substance of the faculty is, but that he infers from its works that it exists, then again this very man in his turn, when asked whether he has examined and refuted what has been written [515] by Asclepiades and many Asclepiadeans and Methodists to the effect that there is no faculty in living beings, appears not even to know whether it has been said by them. Again, as for those very men who say that the faculty does not exist, it is rather more evident that they deny that plethora is conceived and constituted in relation to it; for it is impossible for plethora to be constituted and conceived with reference to a relation that does not exist at all. Instead they suppose that the much and the little exist only in relation to the spaces of the vessels. And sometimes they do not even name plethora at all in the first place, nor do they take from it any indication of evacuation, but only from constriction; and that none of them explains this in the same way has been shown in other works.

And indeed there is also a third band, a different one, which neither knows whether there is or is not some faculty, nor agrees to inquire into it, but asserts that, upon certain signs that appear clearly and arise in the patient, evacuation has been found by it from long experience. Then, when asked what [516] these signs are, it says: distension of the vessels, and redness and heaviness of the whole body, sluggishness towards movements, and tensions of the limbs. Some of them also add the ulcerous and lassitude-like sensation, and an idle previous way of life with rather large intakes of foods and drinks, and retention of the habitual excretions. Upon this syndrome, at any rate (for so they call the aggregate of the symptoms), venesection has been observed to be beneficial. These people, then, deprive not only themselves but all other men as well of reason, asserting that everything has been found from experience. The others, as was said just now, say that they use reason, and concerning the faculty some say that it does not exist at all, others that it does exist but that what its substance is is not known. So those who dare to declare both the existence and the substance of a faculty are very few.

But not even all of these declare the same number of the faculty, or the same substance. Indeed, among those who have left us treatises, some, rather carelessly, always discourse as though about one single faculty governing the animal, [517] adding no reasoning; others attempt to demonstrate it, and say that there are not more than one. So it necessarily follows that whoever declares that there is plethora in the body of the patient has already departed both from the physicians called Empiricists and from the Methodists; and that he speaks of 'the much' either in relation to the faculty or in relation to the vessels. Accordingly, let our argument against the Empiricists and Methodists be deferred, and let us go on to the others, those who say that they practise the art with reasoning. And yet some of those of the present day have arrived at such audacity that they inscribe upon themselves the names of a sect, yet know nothing even of those very things (ἐστὶν). At any rate, one can often hear many of them saying, at the bedside of the sick, that the man is full and must be phlebotomized; and then again, when the subject comes up in discussion, calling themselves Methodists or Empiricists. But, as I was saying, coming to those who use analogism, let us first argue with those of them who always conceive 'the much' in relation to the faculty.

For these men are likely [518] never to have seen wineskins, nor sacks filled beyond measure; nor indeed ever to have taken more food than is needful, so as to distend the stomach, nor ever to have collected urine in the bladder beyond what is fitting, or faeces in the rectum. For in all such circumstances each of the organs mentioned is manifestly distended, so that the person is distressed unless he quickly excretes what is in excess. Nor, indeed, does the same sensation arise from what weighs down, or bites, or causes distress by some indescribable quality. One can, at any rate, hear even laymen clearly expressing what is happening to them, without contentiousness about doctrine: sometimes saying that they are weighed down and oppressed by nourishment, even though they have taken very little; sometimes that they are being bitten and eaten through; and often, not being able to express precisely what is happening, they say that they feel nauseated. For none of these sensations is the same in people as that which arises when, through an immoderate quantity of foods, the stomach is stretched out and distended to the utmost.

In such states, then, they say that their belly is in danger of [519] bursting, and at the same time we ourselves see it stretched to the utmost; but where they say they are weighed down, we sometimes see the stomach drawn in. So too in the case of the bladder, one condition is that of a bladder containing a very great quantity of fluid, and another that of one containing little, that is, of one that is weighed down. And accordingly one can see that the excretion, too, is very copious in the bladder that is stretched because it has been filled, but in the one that is weighed down it is very scanty, though very frequent. For it does not wait for the time of its filling, but longs to throw off at once what is troubling it, just as also when it is bitten by its quality; for then too it makes its excretion continuous. And indeed, whenever it is weighed down as if by a load of what it contains, one could not then rightly say that it is merely in a bad condition, rather than that what weighs it down is much for it, even if it does not distend its coat at all.

But if the leaders of this opinion say these things, or anything at all, while those who hold the contrary view deny it, both must again be asked whether the bladder suffers the same distress when it is distended in every direction and in danger [520] of rupturing, because it can no longer contain what it holds, as when it is weighed down and bitten. For here again those who always conceive plethora in relation to the capacities of the vessels readily concede the point; but those who conceive it as relative to the faculty are vexed at such questions and grow angry, resisting in manifold ways, up and down, because they do not wish to concede that this too is plethora. We, then, having prayed that both parties would cease from their contentiousness, have called them to concord. We urge those who hold that plethora is never spoken of in relation to the space of the container, with whom indeed we first began our discussion, to concede what is true, recalling that the filled parts suffer distress in being distended. We urge those who think that plethora arises only in this way to concede that what weighs down is much for that which is weighed down.

Again, putting each party to shame with what plainly appears, let us remind separately those who assert that 'much' is conceived only in relation to the capacity (dynamis) of the peritoneum torn, or stretched wide by a quantity of foods. Let us also show them, among things outside the body, wineskins and bladders [521] suffering this, and sometimes even the storage jars themselves, when the plethora is pneumatic and violent. And let us ask, about those who have coughed up blood from the lung through rupture of a vessel, without a blow, or a fall, or some other such violence from outside, whether not even these seem to them to have suffered thus through a very great plethora distending the vessel. Separately, in turn, let us remind the others that a youth in good condition and a quite small child cannot carry the same weight; for what would, I think, be heaviest for the child is lightest for the youth. Shall we then say that what someone cannot carry is not a load at all, nor that what weighs down in this way is 'much'? Or shall we allow that it is a load and heavy, yet not allow it to be named plethora? But in this way the dispute will be not about a thing but about a name. In the other way, the man who asserts that he is never weighed down at all, not even if you put twenty talents on his shoulder, would not seem to you even to be a human being. But against those who have subjected themselves to a slavish doctrine nothing is sufficient.

Leaving these men aside now, or rather, if one must [522] tell the truth, bidding them be gone, let us converse with whoever is free and a companion of truth. For we posited two conceptions and relations of plethora: the one with respect to the strength and faculty of that which carries it, the other with respect to the space that receives it. And having posited these, let us examine how many in all are the faculties of the animal, and how we shall either recognise or treat the plethora relative to each of them; and, in addition to these, how many in all are the kinds of the humours themselves, whether of those that weigh down the faculty or of those that are not held in the vessels. For it is in these matters that the physician must be industrious and great, not in despising the evident things, which are the principles of all demonstration. But perhaps it is no wonder that this very thing is unknown to those who have examined nothing concerning demonstration, and have neither discovered it, nor learned it, nor practised it.

So simple-minded, at any rate, are they that even now anyone who engages with these writings expects, first, that I shall demonstrate in this treatise the things which anyone who intends to examine anything about plethora [523] with precision must by all means know; and second, that I shall find the diagnosis and treatment of each plethora. He does not realise that, if matters so great were by nature such as to be demonstrated through a single writing, the art would not be long. I, for my part, demonstrated in my work On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato that the power in the arteries is a different one from that in the nerves and the veins. Through the same treatise I also taught that of the power of the arteries the heart is, as it were, a kind of source, of that of the nerves the brain, and of that of the veins the liver. In my work On the Elements according to Hippocrates I demonstrated that the substance which underlies generation and corruption is altered throughout its whole extent according to the four qualities, moistness and dryness, heat and coldness; that the proper substance of each of the bodies consists in a particular kind of mixture of these; and that for this reason the specific character of the mixture is also the substance of the powers which govern them. This has been shown by me also in the work On Natural Powers, and separately by means of another treatise.

Diagnostic signs have also been stated many times already in many [524] treatises, both for each of the two kinds of plethora and for each of the forms under either kind individually. By 'each of the two' I mean that which is relative to the faculty and that which is by the infused content (enchyma); for so they call the other kind of plethora, which is measured against the space that contains it, and which arises not only in living beings but no less also in inanimate things: in woven fabrics and plaited work, in skins, and in vessels of earthenware, of bronze and of iron, and whatever is made of bronze, silver and tin. For these too burst when a large quantity of pneumatic substance is shut up within them. Unless, that is, someone should wish to say that this kind of plethora also arises relative to the cohesive faculty, forgetting the notion we mentioned at the beginning in connection with the name 'faculty', when we said that it is an active cause, it making no difference whether one says 'active' or 'efficient'.

Nor do we object if someone should wish to say that the faculty is a substance rather than an efficient cause; we wish only this to be preserved in the argument: that it is called active and efficient, and that the faculty is not a passive and material either [525] cause or substance. For if this at least is preserved, it is evident that the faculty will be the cause of some activity; and the activity must surely itself be a motion from the agent into the patient, just as the affection is the motion in the patient from the agent (into the patient); so that the conception of the faculty lies in the category of relation, and its existence in its relation to something else. To say that anything acts upon itself, or is active upon itself, is contrary to the notion; and so too, then, that anything holds itself together. For even those who most of all introduced the cohesive faculty, such as the Stoics, make that which holds together one thing and that which is held together another: the pneumatic substance is what holds together, the material substance what is held together. Hence they say that air and fire hold together, while earth and water are held together.

And yet some of those who nowadays call themselves Herophileans, never having heard of these things even in a dream, make bold pronouncements about the cohesive power. They admit that they do not know whether it is air, or fire, or the two together that holds together stones and pieces of wood and all other such things; [526] but they declare simply that it is some power that holds together all such things, since these would be dissolved and would flow apart if nothing drew them together and bound them tight. Then, when asked whether they also dare to use in their argument some such axiom as that all existing things need something that holds them together, or not, they at once readily declare for it and affirm the question. But when they are led on from there to an absurdity, they take back what they have said, and become indignant with those who question them, calling them meddlesome and sophists. For this, if anything, is a practised skill among present-day physicians: to pronounce readily on the most important doctrines, but, when refuted, to be vexed and to call those who refute them sophists. How, then, the argument must necessarily be led to some absurdity once we posit that everything that exists needs a cohesive cause, I shall now go through for you. The cohesive cause, whatever it may be (for the Herophileans do not admit to knowing it): do they themselves suppose it to be one of the things that exist, or one of the things that do not exist?

For if it is one of the things that are not, I marvel at the [527] wisdom of these men, if they say that each of the things that are also needs one of the things that are not. But if they place the containing cause among the things that are, let them recall that they said that everything that is needs a containing cause in order to be. For in this way it will follow that the cause itself also needs another cause in order that it may exist, and that one in turn another, and so on to infinity. But if they say that, of the things that are, some need some other cause in order to be, while others have their being from themselves, then first let them know that they are no longer preserving the axiom from which they began, which they declared to be true above all else, namely that everything that is needs a containing cause in order to be; and second, that they stand in need of a very lengthy account of why some things need it and others do not, or indeed of what sort the things in each of these two classes are. For neither the majority of the Herophileans nor the more recent Stoics state any demonstration that pneuma and fire hold together both themselves and the other things, while water and earth need something else to hold them together.

For so far as the immediate impression goes, what is hard, resistant and dense might be said to hold itself together, and what is rare [528] and soft and yielding to need something else to hold it together. Yet not only do these men, having stated no demonstration at all, expect their hypothesis to be believed, but they also fail to notice that the hypothesis they posit is in conflict with itself. For the things that are of all the finest in their parts, the softest and the most yielding, namely fire and air, these, they say, are the causes to earth of its hardness and resistance, as though it were possible for one thing to impart to some other thing a faculty, or a nature, or an activity, or a quality in which it does not itself partake. And indeed it is, moreover, plainly seen not only that nothing is held together by fire, but that all things are dissolved by it. Against the hypothesis of the Stoics, then, the case has been argued at greater length elsewhere; I return to the Herophileans, and against them it will suffice me, for the present at least, to say that their leader has fared in the most contrary way: he professes perplexity in a great many matters that have ready demonstrations, but makes positive declarations in others whose demonstrations are impossible and whose hypothesis is false.

[529] Leaving these men too aside, then, let us say again that being distended and ruptured on account of plethora is an affection of the containing vessels themselves, not of any faculty; whereas being weighed down is an affection of the sensory faculty. For not even this belongs, simply, to every faculty: at any rate, being weighed down is not an affection of the natural faculty. If, then, we rightly demonstrated in the treatise on the natural faculties that there is one faculty attractive of what is proper, another alterative of these same things, another a retentive faculty, and a fourth eliminative of what is foreign, then one must seek certain other signs of the plethora relative to each of the faculties mentioned, since the heaviness is not sufficient. For it is not the case that, just as the weak stomach perceives the things that weigh it down, on account of the superabundance of its sensation, so too the vein and the artery have the same sensation; rather, they have a different one. If, then, it is a kind not the same as that in the nerves, this requires a longer account for its exposition and proof.

Now, for the plethora in the arteries, relative to their faculty, scientific distinguishing marks [530] have been stated in the treatise on the pulses; but those who glibly name plethora every day know not even one of these. For the plethora relative to the veins, however, I have neither discovered any scientific sign myself nor been able to find one written down by anyone else, since no one before us had, to begin with, even defined the faculties themselves scientifically. Philippus and Archigenes and their followers did touch a little upon the theory of them, but not even any of these worked it out completely. The present discussion, however, seeks not only these things but also the plethora in each part, for instance that in the liver, or the heart, or the kidneys, or a limb, or the brain, or a bone. Now those of them that are either of dull sensation or insensible would not perceive the superfluities in them in the same way as the stomach and the bladder do: the latter group would not perceive them at all, and the former either quite faintly or not at all. They perceive them quite faintly when the plethora is very great, and not at all when it is small.
