For in fact a sensation of heaviness sometimes arises in the lung, the liver and the kidneys as well, and someone has perceived a bone being weighed down, he too with a faint sensation; but in the [531] brain heavinesses often make themselves felt not only faintly, but they are sometimes even quite distinct. In the insensible parts, however, it is not possible for any sensation to arise, neither of heaviness nor of any other symptom; and some of the bones, the fat, and certain of the glands seem to be insensible, unless indeed all the marrows too are among the insensible parts; the brain at any rate and the spinal [marrow], as some say, are among the sensitive parts. One could make a firm declaration regarding the flesh at the convex parts of the liver, which most physicians call parenchyma; for no nerve at all is implanted into it from anywhere. But one might be in doubt also about the [flesh] in the concave parts. For the [nerves] implanted into the liver at the portae are so small that they appear to interweave only its membrane.

And indeed one might likewise be at a loss about the spleen and the kidneys, and still more about the lung. Perhaps, whatever sensation of heaviness there is in these viscera might be said to belong not to the viscera themselves but to the tunics and membranes that enclose them, and especially in the case of the lung and the [532] liver, which are attached and hang suspended and are not firmly fixed in place. For patients often clearly perceive a certain tension up near the collarbone, as with swellings in the liver, when the viscus itself is heavy; and fortunate indeed is anyone who has not perceived this in the whole of his life, so constantly does it occur in everyone. Hippocrates too says somewhere, 'into the kidney a heavy pain', just as heaviness also occurs in the lung; and this has been stated by almost all physicians, whenever the viscus is seized by inflammation. But most physicians, having investigated none of these matters, and some not even realising that plethora can sometimes be in the whole animal but can also occur in any one part, or even in several, pronounce rashly about plethora. But, if you will, let us for the present leave aside all these problems and exercise ourselves on the easier ones. It seems to me easier to begin once more from heaviness; for this appears to be the clearest sign of plethora relative to the sensory faculty.

Is it, [533] then, true to declare that heaviness follows upon plethora of necessity, or that heaviness of necessity precedes plethora? For it is certainly not the same thing for heaviness to follow in the argument or to precede. It is true that whoever has a plethora of certain fluids in the body has a sensation of heaviness, evidently in those parts in which the plethora is, if they are sensitive. But it is not true that, when there is heaviness in some part, there is a plethora of humours in it. For it is possible for the faculty, when it is weak, to be weighed down by the solid parts, as in paralyses. For when the whole limb is moved by the muscles, and the muscles become too weak to move and carry it, a sensation of heaviness arises in those who are paralysed.

For what is weak does not appear heavy to itself, for instance the muscle, or the nerve, or in general whatever body it may be that primarily moves the parts. Rather, this affection that is called heaviness naturally arises in some things from something else. And the nerve itself, by itself, or the tendon, or the muscle, or whatever it may be that moves us, may become of weaker tone than itself [534] and feebler, but to weigh itself down is among the things that are impossible. If, then, it becomes of better tone, it will make its activities stronger than before; if of weaker tone, weaker. For example the muscle, if indeed it is this that moves the leg, will when healthy draw vigorously that part of the limb into which it is inserted, and when in good condition most vigorously; when diseased, feebly; and when it is enfeebled in its capacity, faintly. But if it is not the muscle but the nerve that moves the muscle itself, then again the health and disease, the good condition and weakness of that nerve will produce in the limb the very effects that the muscle was said to produce. In the same way, if the pneuma too is the first of the things that move the leg, these same things will be said of it. Come then, for the sake of clarity let the following be laid down by us: that the muscle is moved by the pneuma carried through the nerves; and that by the muscle is moved first the lower leg, into which the muscle is inserted, and then, through the lower leg, the articulation at the knee, upon which the whole leg is set.

For on these hypotheses one might truly say that the muscle itself becomes a weight to the enfeebled pneuma, and together with it the whole limb, for instance, [535] the lower leg. But if we suppose that the nerve is moved by the pneuma, and the muscle by the nerve, and then in turn the lower leg by the muscle, the enfeebled pneuma will be weighed down by all of the things mentioned. So it is already clear here too that it is not possible to diagnose what primarily weighs down and what is weighed down without first knowing what primarily moves each of the parts in us. But this too we shall examine more precisely later; let the subject the discussion was about be brought to completion. For the sake of clarity the whole exposition will proceed on a hypothesis. Let it therefore be supposed that the muscle is what primarily moves both itself and the bone of the lower leg.

To itself, then, it is never heavy, not even when it is in its most atonic state; but the shin weighs it down. Whether it does so only when it seeks to be moved, or even when it is at rest, would be a matter for another inquiry, and no small one, which we have determined in the books On the Movement of Muscles. Without that inquiry it is not possible to diagnose exactly, from the sensations of heaviness, either the condition or the affected place. For instance, in some people either a single limb or even [536] the whole body is weighed down when they have chosen to move, but while they are at rest no sensation of heaviness arises; others say they are weighed down even before moving. What, then, the condition of each of these is, it is impossible to know before one has discovered the moving and the moved bodies throughout the whole leg. For if the fibres of the nerves in the muscle are the first to be moved, and along with them there are moved within it the membranous kind, the venous, the arterial, and further the ligaments, then a sensation of heaviness will arise for it both because of these and because of all the other things throughout the whole limb. We shall examine and determine when the heaviness will occur while the limb is acting and being moved, and when while it is at rest. But if the kind of the ligaments within it is also moved together with the fleshy part (for these are the proper substance of the muscle), then the sensation of heaviness could never arise through any of these. It will arise either from the veins, or from the arteries, or from the fat, or from the bones, or from some of them, or from all.

It is clear that, even if in divisions of this kind we should at some point leave out the 'from some' or 'from all', those [537] reading the book must understand it as supplied, knowing that in all such statements the conjunctions are used not disjunctively but subdisjunctively. From what has been said, then, it is quite clear that whoever wishes to be capable of diagnosing a plethoric part must have knowledge of the faculties that govern us, and also of the anatomy and nature of all the parts of the animal, precisely; for, starting out from this, he might perhaps at some point discover signs of a plethoric part. But if someone has given no thought to the truth, and wishes instead to deceive those around him into thinking that he has come to know something clever, it is open to him, if nothing else, at least to learn what Erasistratus says in the first book of his Hygiene; for nowhere else did he so much as attempt to state signs of plenitude. Let us then attend to his words: first those in which he says what the origin of plethora is (for this is what he himself calls the plenitude in the veins), and then, next, those in which he sets out the signs for its diagnosis. Now the origin, according to him, is as follows.

"For when the food that is being distributed is neither concocted, nor worked off [538] in the manner customary for each person, nor excreted in some other way, the vessels must necessarily be filled, while concoction and distribution (and) perform the activities proper to them. And since the food already present in the vessels is in no way used up, while food from what is ingested is added to it, the vessels in the body are distended still further. And when the vessels no longer admit any further packing-in, and other food is brought up from the stomach, what is present gains an impetus into the adjacent vessels of the pneuma." From this, then, it is clear that he is discussing the plenitude in respect of the contents poured into the vessels (enchyma), and also from his calling it, in the specific sense, plethora; for only this affection is named plethora, not the other one, which is judged relative to the strength. A little further on, in discussing its diagnosis, he writes the following: "It is necessary, therefore, as has been said, to try to diagnose the condition of plethora."

At its beginning, then, when the vessels are moderately filled, people appear of better tone and stronger than themselves, contrary to what is customary. But as the vessels come to a greater degree of filling, the arms, legs and hands become filled up besides [539], as in those who come into distension after exercise. And when the plethora advances a long way, they are ulcerous, slower and harder to move, and the whole touch of the body is tense, as when fatigue appears. Such a condition is already close to disease, unless someone resolves it very dexterously and intelligently. In these words Erasistratus confounded the signs of plethoras of different kinds, and in addition he also wrote into them some things that are not necessary. One may examine his account from the beginning. For in the words 'At its beginning, then, when the vessels are moderately filled, people appear of better tone and stronger than themselves, contrary to what is customary', the account has a necessary consequence in neither direction: neither from the condition to its signs, nor from the signs to the condition. For it is neither necessary that, when the vessels are moderately filled, people appear of better tone and stronger than themselves, nor, when they appear such, have the vessels been moderately filled.

For with moderate fillings of these it is possible that some people sometimes even [540] become of poorer tone, or change to no perceptible degree in neither direction, neither towards strength nor towards weakness; and if they become stronger than before, it is possible in their case not only that the quantity of the humours has increased along with the capacity, but also sometimes that it has diminished, and sometimes that it keeps its original quantity. For on either supposition it is possible for what was stated first to have three things following from it: upon the humours' having increased there may follow good tone, or lack of tone, compared with the previous condition, or again the persistence of the capacity within the same limits; and upon a person's having become of better tone there may follow the humours' having increased, or their having diminished, or their being in due proportion. In the present discussion let it be understood in the same way whether I say 'humours' or 'blood'; for a distinction will be drawn concerning them as the discussion proceeds. Erasistratus, then, made a bare assertion, appending no demonstration to what he said; but we, not barely, but confirming each of the things we have just said with necessary demonstrations, shall here too once again make our beginning from Erasistratus' very words: 'they appear', he says, 'of better tone and stronger'.

[541] Does 'more well-toned' (εὐτονώτεροι) signify something other than 'stronger' (ἰσχυρότεροι), so that he has taught us two signs of moderate plethos? Or did he state two names but only one sign? For my part, I find no difference in what is signified, neither in genus, nor in species, nor in the more and less; I hold that the same thing is signified by each. If you like, suppose that the one term displays an intensification and increase relative to the other, whether 'stronger' relative to 'more well-toned' or 'more well-toned' relative to 'stronger'. Even so, what is signified by both is certainly of the same species. And where there is an increase while the species remains, there is no teaching of two things signified. It is quite clear that Erasistratus does not even mention at all the other genus of plethos, the one that is relative to the capacity (δύναμις), neither in this book nor in his works on fevers.

For according to him plethora is the cause of paremptosis, upon which inflammations arise and fever follows. He clearly set out the genesis of plethora in the passage quoted earlier, where he says that the vessels in the body are packed full and are distended [542] to the utmost. He himself used these very words, just as he also said that, because the vessels can no longer take up the packing, a paremptosis of the superfluity into the arteries takes place, the things that abound in the veins having taken their impetus there. Here too, then, something has been left out in the division. He should not have said so simply that, when the veins no longer receive the packing, the impetus of what is in them is directed into the vessels of the pneuma. It would have been much better to say that one of two things follows the aforementioned filling of the veins: either a rupture of its coat, or a transfusion of the blood into the vessels of the pneuma. To suppose that the blood is of necessity transfused because it is not contained by the veins is the mark of someone who has entirely forgotten that rupture of a vessel sometimes occurs through plethos. I pass over the anastomosis without transfusion that often plainly occurs into perceptible cavities: those of the intestines, the stomach, the gullet, the pharynx and the mouth.

But this deficiency in the division of the arguments [543] is habitual to Erasistratus not only in this work but also in almost all his other treatises. Let us, then, examine again the statement itself, whatever it may be. "When the vessels are moderately filled, people appear in better tone than they themselves were." Is this so, Erasistratus, even if the strength of the body does not increase together with the quantity of the blood, or only when it too increases along with it? For my part, I say that for the good tone of the activity it is most necessary that the strength of the faculty also be increased. And so, if you believe that the activities of the faculty become stronger through the increase of the blood alone, you would seem to overturn the faculties more than Asclepiades does. For not even he says, in this simple way, that whoever has more blood is in every case in better tone, and whoever has less is of necessity in poorer tone; rather, you will find him stating certain qualifying distinctions that agree with the phenomena, even though he holds that there is no faculty in us, either psychic or vital.

For some people are seen who have at times become both fuller of blood and stronger than they were before [544], and others who have become both stronger and less full of blood. So, since strength is necessarily neither increased by the quantity of the blood nor brought down by its diminution, we must consider that these things too were stated rather carelessly by Erasistratus. For if someone had reminded him of what I have now gone through, he would not have denied that the vigour of the functions follows not upon an increase of the blood but upon the robustness of the faculty. Let us, then, now make his argument more complete ourselves, adding what is lacking to what he stated deficiently. It will be as follows: when the blood is increased together with the faculty, the vigour too must necessarily be increased. And yet, even if we should say this, we shall be saying something true, but not even from this shall we gain anything more toward the matters before us.

For it will be said truly that in those in whom both have increased together, the blood and the faculty, the good tone also has increased; but that in those in whom what pertains to strength has increased, both have of necessity increased, is false. For the faculty does not of necessity increase together with the blood when the blood has increased, and it is possible sometimes for the faculty alone to increase. [545] At any rate the truly good gymnastic trainer, if he should take over someone who from lack of exercise has accumulated much phlegmatic blood but is rather weak in faculty, will in a short while render him stronger, not more full of blood, than he was when he took him over. Just as, then, it is not necessary that those who have become of better tone in their activities than they themselves were should have had their humours increased, so it is necessary that those who have become of better tone in their activities than they themselves were should have had their faculty become stronger. And not only, starting from the good tone, will you of necessity proceed by consequence to the robustness of the faculty, but also from the faculty to the good tone; for the man who is strong in faculty is of better tone in his activities. So good tone in the activities and robustness of faculty follow reciprocally upon one another, good tone in the activities upon robustness of faculty, and robustness in the faculty upon good tone of the activities; for whichever of the two you suppose to be present, the other is in every case present together with it. From a greater quantity of blood, however, the consequence is not necessary.

For neither, if this is more than before, is the person of necessity more vigorous, nor, if less, more lacking in vigour, just as neither, when it is equal, is he in the same [546] condition as regards capacity. So from what has been said it is clear that the vigour of the activities is a sign at once peculiar to and inseparable from the capacity's being strong, but of the increase of the blood it is neither peculiar nor inseparable. What Erasistratus said next, however, is not peculiar to plethora, but is inseparable from it. He names it 'being filled up' (parempímplasthai), but it would be named more clearly 'being stretched'. And indeed the more precise among the trainers, calling one of the fatigues ulcerative, another tensive, and another inflammatory, indicate nothing other than the limbs' being filled up in the tensive fatigue. For they say that any part whatever of themselves has been filled up at the time when they perceive some tension in it. Now they perceive tension in inflammation as well; but with that there is present, either always or for the most part, the pulsation contrary to nature, which someone expressing it more vividly will call a pulsating pain. In those, however, to whom nothing else has happened except being stretched, the part that is stretched is neither inflamed nor of necessity plethoric, but one of two things: either fatigued or plethoric.

But if [547] it is fatigued, it has been so affected after rather many exertions; whereas if the person has not exerted himself at all, the part itself becomes fatigued not through fatigue but in some other way. So it is true to say that, since there is a perception of tension without one's having exercised, there is in every case plethora. And when it is stated in this way, the sign becomes at the same time both inseparable and proper, the two following each other of necessity. For tension without exercise follows upon plethora, since it becomes an inseparable sign of it, as being brought about by plethora as its cause; while an increase of the blood to such a degree as not yet to distend the veins is not yet plethora. Why, then, did Erasistratus in his account make mention of arms and shins and hands? For such tension also arises in the neck, the upper back, the loins, the chest and the hypogastrium.

Just as Erasistratus mentioned the limbs superfluously, in the same way, and still more so, did he mention the ulcerous sensation. For this is not a mark of plethora; it arises with biting humours, such as occurs in ulcerated parts, whether something touches them, or ichor irritates them, [548] or a biting drug, or it arises even in movements alone. For just as tension is proper to an abundance of humours that stretch what contains them, so the ulcerous sensation follows a biting quality. For this reason it sometimes arises in many people even over the whole body, people who not only do not have plethora but do not even have the due measure of blood. And if these things are so, as indeed they are, it is now time to determine something about one of the matters we postponed earlier, since up to this point we were examining the signs written down by Erasistratus. For the plethos, whether it be conceived in relation to the capacity or in relation to the space of what contains it, it would surely have been better to determine whether it naturally arises in blood alone or also in all the other humours. But this too has been left undetermined by them.

Since, then, the humours are seized not only by these affections, deficiency and plenitude, but also by an abnormal quality, I asked all the physicians, both those who conceive of plenitude in relation to the capacity and those who conceive of it in relation to the increase of the fluids, whether, [549] if the blood alone has increased so much that it is not contained, it will happen that the veins are stretched; but if either phlegm into any other part whatever, or into the veins themselves, or, either together with this or apart from it, some bile, or ichor, or flatulent pneuma should be collected into a quantity so great that it can no longer be held by what surrounds it, will it not be necessary in this case too that the animal perceive tension? If the part being stretched is capable of sensation, it is necessary that, in the case of everything that distends and is not contained, the perception of tension arises for the animal, and that the affection itself seizes the parts, the one called tension; and when this increases further, it is necessary that the part being stretched also ruptures. To me, at any rate, such a view seems to agree with what is evidently apparent. For not only sinews or ropes are seen bursting from the violence of the tension, but often jars as well, through must that has become filled with pneuma.

Recently, at any rate, a tin vessel was so inflated by the drug contained in it, the one made from vipers, that both the skin placed around it and the cord with which it had been tied down burst, and [550] the lid was bulged outwards. Moreover, I think that all who take care to follow and examine what is seen day by day in patients know that some people are sometimes seized by very great pains when flatulent pneuma is trapped in certain parts of the animal, and that this is accustomed to happen most of all in the colon. It is better, then, to hold that the parts are brought into a tensive condition by every moist and pneumatic substance than that such an affection follows upon blood alone among the humours when it is in excess. Let us therefore pass over once more to those who think that plethora always arises in relation to the strength, and let us ask them too one of the most obvious things, positing a supposition of the following kind, by way of example.

(parts) Let two men carry, having placed it upon their shoulders, the one a log, or a stone, or some very heavy load, the other a very few, very sharp thorns. Then, at such a spectacle, let us ask those who always conceive of plethora in relation to the strength whether they also call the few thorns a load, or whether being distressed by each of the things carried [551] is a symptom common to the men, while the form of the distress differs very greatly: for it has befallen the one to be weighed down without being pricked, the other to be pricked without being weighed down. And in general, if someone calls being pricked, or being bitten, or what causes distress in any way whatever a load and a plethora, he will at some point be compelled to call even a single thorn or a very fine needle a load; and what could be more ridiculous than this? These things, then, are absurd and contrary to the common notions of all men. Our purpose, however, is not to overturn but to preserve the common notions. We therefore regard what weighs down as 'much', and what bites, or pricks, or however one may wish to name it, as distressing. And indeed that many of the humours are biting, some having their origin within ourselves, others being brought upon us from outside, this is evident to everyone.

There are four differences among them according to the more and the less. Those that bite moderately are itch-producing, as squill is; those that bite more vehemently are mordant, as the onion is; for if our body were to be in contact for longer with a body of such a nature, it will be ulcerated. [552] Things still more acrid than this, especially when they are applied to ulcerated parts, produce shivering; and when shivering is prolonged and intensified, the symptom is called rigor. By the same analogy, mordant humours form in us in four kinds. Those of them that scratch moderately are itch-producing; those more mordant than these produce an ulcerous sensation; those that bite more than these, shivering; and those that are exceedingly mordant, rigor. These matters have been discussed in many treatises, but for anyone who wishes to get a synopsis of them, what is said in the second book of the Causes in Symptoms and in the fourth of the Hygiene is sufficient. If someone were also to read through the treatise on the power of drugs, and the treatise that precedes it, the one on mixtures, he would in this way be persuaded in a more scientific manner about the nature of mordant things.

But most physicians have suffered something similar to what was said by Hippocrates about those who, in fractures or some such affections, do not do what is prescribed. For they too, although wishing to become healthy, [553] do not endure the toil involved in the treatment, just as these do not endure the toil involved in learning. But it is neither possible to become healthy all at once, attaining the end by merely wishing it, nor for these men to become scientifically knowledgeable without traversing the whole road which I have just now indicated. For they will recognise, if they are willing, that the ulcerous sensation of the whole body, both that which arises upon rather many exercises undertaken in an unaccustomed manner and that which comes on suddenly without exercises, is the offspring of a biting humour. And for this reason the trainers treat those who have exercised too much with more oil, soft rubbing, and hot baths of sweet waters, exactly well-tempered, so that the biting humours may be dispersed: those which, in people who have exercised rather immoderately, were generated upon a colliquation of fat and soft flesh, or on account of the humours in the body themselves having been strongly heated.

If, then, anyone should persevere in learning the demonstrations of these things thoroughly, he alone would be firmly persuaded that the ulcerous condition arises from biting humours; that of heaviness from humours that are many in relation to the capacity; and that of tension from humours that are, this too, many, but [554] in relation to the space that contains them, not to the capacity of the (contained) bodies. Erasistratus, in the first book of his *Hygieina*, while going through the very genesis of plethora, teaches the third of the conditions mentioned most clearly; but turning next to the signs, he wrote those of this one no more than those of the others. For tension belongs to this one alone, which is what he called 'being over-filled'. But the sensation becoming ulcerous is a proper sign neither of the plenitude just mentioned nor of that in relation to the capacity; and much less still is becoming heavier and more sluggish in movement such a sign, for this too is proper to the plenitude in relation to the capacity.

He very nearly, then, wrote out for us the whole syndrome of the Empirics. Indeed, he also wrote a certain part of the so-called three-time semeiosis, which Herophilus and his followers introduced, as the Empirics also did, when he spoke thus: 'For when the nourishment that is distributed is neither concocted nor worked off by exertion in the way customary for each person, nor excreted in any other way'. It made no difference whether one says this or, as they say, [555] 'an idle life and retention of the customary excretions'. For he indicated the idle previous life by saying 'nor worked off by exertion in the way customary for each person', and the retention of the excretions by adding 'nor excreted in any other way' (the semeiosis of the plenitude through time). From the time that has gone before he takes the idle life together with the retention of the excretions. From the time now present he takes the being overfilled and the ulcerous condition, reluctance towards movements, heaviness of the whole body, and whatever other such things they add. From the future he takes the fact that those in this state are much benefited when they have been evacuated, and this Erasistratus has omitted. For this is a testimony to correct diagnosis and therapy together. But it would be no part of diagnosis, or, as they call it, semeiosis, if indeed we wish through semeiosis to signify the conditions so that we may find the appropriate therapy. So if it were possible to treat appropriately by starting from something else, semeiosis would be superfluous.

While making mention of the present time, he has omitted redness and distension of the vessels [556], which almost all the Empiricists add as well, and not a few of the Dogmatists, just as they add certain other things too, as has been said. And yet, for those who suppose that the genesis of plethora is in the blood alone, it is not badly that the redness and the distension of the vessels are added to the diagnosis in their case. And still more so for him, since he will take the statement that the arms, hands and shins are overfilled as a sign no more of the plethos in the fleshes and in the whole muscles than of that of the veins, following his own hypotheses. But even so it was necessary to make a twofold diagnosis: one of the plethos of these perceptible veins, which all of us human beings see; the other of that which he alone beheld. I think, then, that it has by now become quite plain, at least to those who pay attention, that to diagnose plethos is no small matter. And where it is not easy to diagnose it even as far as reasoning goes, but it is in every way a matter of perplexity, hardly would it be got right in practice by chance by those who have neither examined anything about it beforehand nor found it out.

[557] Let us, then, begin the account of plethos once again from the Empiricists, since they seem to escape the difficulties mentioned quite safely: they themselves admit that they know nothing at all about the essence of plethos, but they claim that in a certain syndrome of this kind the withdrawal of blood has been observed to be beneficial, and this syndrome they call plethoric. For they gather together into one all that has been said by each of the Dogmatists, and they think that in this way they escape the difficulties of those men; but they are refuted far more than the Dogmatists are, if one attends to what they say. It is better to go through all of this again from the beginning.

Let it be supposed, then, that in the preceding time the regimen was the customary one, consisting of the foods taken from the beginning, and, with some of them, in greater repletion than before; that there was retention of excretion; and that the whole manner of life was idle. And let it be supposed that at present there is tension of the whole body, or of certain parts; reluctance towards movements; lack of tone in the activities; and a sensation of heaviness and of an ulcerous condition, together with distension of the veins. Let there be added, if you wish, redness as well, since some [558] mention this too; and moreover the distension of the whole body, and a certain uneven and lassitudinous condition, for there are those who add these too. We shall therefore ask them what I, as a youth, asked my Empiric teacher when he first taught me these things: must all the things mentioned concur at once for what they themselves call the 'recollection' of evacuation, or, even if they observe just one of them, will they at once perform venesection? To the first question he readily answered me, saying that all must concur, for the syndrome is just such a thing: an aggregate of all the things that make it up.

But when I first reminded him of two men whom he himself had recently ordered to be phlebotomized, the one suffering severely from ophthalmia, the other who had fallen from a vehicle and then become entangled in the reins and been dragged a considerable distance, so that some parts were bruised; and when, after this, he fell silent, I recalled another as well, whom he had phlebotomized while he was only moderately feverish but could not bear the pain of the head; and another, a pleuritic, [559] who likewise did not have the whole syndrome that had been stated: he was put into the greatest perplexity. And so I went on at greater length with him, recounting some other similar cases too, and I also reminded him about those already mentioned, that he had phlebotomized them although they fell so far short of having the whole syndrome that I, for my part, said I could not recall even any two of its components being present in these men. For the man who fell from the vehicle, who exercised daily, was adequately evacuated by all his customary excretions, ate in due measure, spent nearly the whole day in our company, and seemed neither to him nor to anyone else to be in need of evacuation, he judged to warrant phlebotomy because, having been thrown down, he was bruised in some parts, although he had acquired neither any redness, nor swelling of the vessels, nor anything else of the components of the syndrome, but only had pain in the bruised parts.

In the same way also the man suffering from ophthalmia and the man suffering pain in the head, who had none at all of the things stated in the plethoric syndrome; and many others too I know to have been bled by us, either having nothing whatever from the plethoric syndrome, [560] or at any rate not all together the things stated by us. "For just now," I said, "recalling to myself those whom I saw bled by you, I cannot find a single one among them who had the complete syndrome in such symptoms. Rather, one was bled because he was in a state of lassitude, having nothing else; another because he was violently feverish, or was suffering pain in the eyes, or in the head, or had had haemorrhoids suppressed, or, being a woman, her menses; but not all the things which the plethoric syndrome requires to concur. If, then, you call plethoric all the conditions in which venesection has been observed to be beneficial, it is time for us to call ophthalmia, pleurisy, violent pain, a fall from a vehicle, and countless other things plethoric syndromes. But if none of these is contained in the plethoric syndrome, and it is the aggregate of the symptoms stated earlier that is called the plethoric syndrome, then one ought to bleed no one before he has all of them."

How that man met me on these points, and gave no fitting answer, would be a task for much leisure, [561] and not a task proper to the matters now before us. Since I have no leisure now for idle talk, I decided not to do it now; rather, in my treatise on venesection I have resolved to set out all the indications of this remedy, which no one has written down with precision and with proper distinctions. Leaving aside for the present, then, the argument against the Empiricists, I return once more to the Rationalists, examining each of the symptoms they have written down. For some of them are signs of plethora relative to the faculty, others of plethora in respect of the contents of the vessels; some are signs not of plethora simply, but of plethora of a particular kind; and some are signs of no plethora at all, but either of cacochymia and corruption, or of a weak faculty, or of increased bulk of the solid bodies. That this is so you will learn if you attend to what is about to be said.

Now the tensive condition, when it occurs without exercises, indicates in every case that much substance is contained in a sentient body; it does not, however, go on to indicate which substance it is, or what its kind is, at least by this alone, the being stretched itself, which is common [562] to all substance: thin, thick, and intermediate in consistency, and pneumatic, and further hot and cold, or intermediate. Rather, it requires certain other distinguishing signs for determining this. Lack of tone in the activities, on the other hand, shows the faculty to be more infirm, in that the moving agent is held back, as in the case of a weak movement of the hands; for it follows upon many states. For if in someone both the fleshy and the fatty kind should be increased while the faculty remains within the same limits, the movements must become more lacking in tone, since the mover remains equal while what is moved has increased. Or if any one of the humours, or even all of them together, should be in excess while the faculty has not increased along with them, then too the activities must become more lacking in tone. Or if both should increase together, the so-called parenchymata and the fluids, but the faculty does not increase along with them; or if, these remaining in the same condition, the faculty should become weaker.

And sometimes both may also come together, so that the faculty becomes weaker [563] and the humours, together with the parenchymata, are either more or fewer, or either one of them, whichever it be. The activities become more lacking in tone for these reasons too, whether each of them occurs singly, or two together, or more, or all at once. For to think that a movement more lacking in tone could ever be produced by the good nourishment of the solid bodies belongs to people who do not know that the faculties pervade the whole of the solid bodies, but who make the arteries and the nerves like pipes or channels for pneuma. You will learn the wrongness of this opinion from many other things, but not least from two treatises of ours, the one On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato and the one On the Natural Faculties. Good nourishment of the solid bodies, then, is proper to good condition (euexia), while increase of the flesh is proper to good fleshiness and excessive fleshiness. For the most part, then, the fat increases more in proportion; but sometimes it is rather the flesh in fat, or fat alone. These things have been discussed in the books On Mixtures.

Just as in flesh there is on the one hand good flesh, on the other abundance of flesh, [564] in the same way in blood there is on the one hand something like a good blood, on the other an abundance of blood. Now as regards good blood, it is not unclear that it is exactly in accordance with nature both in quality and in quantity; that of abundance of blood, however, is blameless in its quality but not blameless in its quantity: it is in every case greater, either than what is in accordance with nature from birth, or than what stands in relation to the capacity. For it is possible at times for both to increase together with one another beyond the nature present from birth, both the strength of the capacity and the quantity of the blood, as in the athletic states of good condition; for in these the moist and the fleshy parts and the capacity increase together in proportion with one another. And so it is by now quite plain that those who have declared the bulk of the body to be one of the plethoric signs do not speak truly either. For bulk of the veins would be a plethoric sign, but bulk of the flesh and of the fat would be an abundance of those things themselves, not, however, the abundance we are now investigating, which is indeed also called plethora.

For, having set out to speak about this plethora, which evidently indicates evacuation, to so great an extent, as it is sometimes [565] indicated by homonymies, some of them went astray, so as to be carried off to the plethora of the flesh and of the fat. So poor a sign of plethora, then, is bulk of the body. Bulk of the veins, for its part, would be indicative of the filling of those very veins that we see, but not necessarily of those in the depth. Rather, it is possible at times that, even when the outer veins are distended, the inner ones are not likewise distended. For instance, when cold has taken hold, the blood is driven into the depth, and the outer veins become so deficient in blood that they do not even appear. Again, when there is warmth, or when people have bathed, the blood is carried to the skin and the outer parts of the body, leaving the depth behind. And if there should be a burning fever, it is necessary that then too it be burnt in the body, as though boiling, and be turned into pneuma and diffused. So bulk of the veins is not an inseparable sign of a plethora of humours. Rather, first, the body must be in such a condition that neither the inner parts exceed the outer, nor the outer the inner, in heat. Second, the heat throughout the whole animal must not be immoderate.

[566] With these distinctions drawn beforehand, the swelling of the veins might at times be a sign of the sanguineous plethora now under discussion, that which is so called by predominance. For it is impossible that blood so exactly pure should ever be contained in the veins that nothing at all is carried along with it, neither of bile, nor of phlegm, nor of serous ichor. For this reason I too, in what preceded, thought it right that it be understood in the same way whether I should say that the humours are in excess or that the blood is. For since blood unmixed and pure of the other fluids is never contained in the veins (this has been shown by us elsewhere), but rather mixed blood, and mixed not at random but with the others mingled into it in a certain due proportion in animals that are in their natural state, it will make no difference whether one calls them humours or blood.

For when all [the humours] increase together, in their natural proportion, with the blood that is [so called] by predominance, the name 'humours' signifies the same thing, and it makes no difference whether one says that the humours have increased or the blood, since the statement that speaks of 'the humours' shows precisely this: that they have in every case become excessive while keeping the original proportion. Let this, then, be determined by us in this way, and let us return again to [567] the matter before us. For the swelling of the veins, if it has come about neither through predominance of the external condition nor through diffusion and boiling, indicates that the plethora is sanguineous.

But such a part must also not have been placed in a dependent posture, nor have been recently exercised more than the others. Therefore one who embraces all the particular distinctions in a single statement will say that the swelling of the veins indicates a plethora of blood at that time when all the parts are in the same condition, with moderate warmth. For if all the parts were disposed alike but the heat were immoderate, a diffusion of the humours occurs in this case which raises the veins into swelling; yet it indicates a plethora that is not sanguineous but pneumatic, for the humours, when heated, are turned into pneuma. Hence also those who declared that the swelling of the veins signifies plethora will seem to have spoken correctly, provided one understands in addition, in the statement, 'in those veins in which this happens to be occurring'. For the substance that has produced the swelling in the veins is necessarily greater than before; yet it is not yet clear of what kind the plethora [568] is. For swelling contrary to nature is common to every abundant substance, whether it be pure blood, or bilious, or serous, or phlegmatic, or pneumatic. And just as this is common to every variety of plethora, so too is the stretching of the veins; for this too follows upon the quantity of the plethora, not upon its difference in kind. So the swelling and the tensive sensation will indicate a plethora of humours no more than one of pneuma. If, then, someone were to declare somewhat as follows: 'where there are tensive sensations there is necessarily plethora', he will speak the truth; and indeed if he should say thus: 'plethora in sensitive parts brings on a certain condition', he too will speak the truth. But if someone, abandoning the generic name 'plethora' or 'the humours', were to substitute 'blood' in the statement, he will not necessarily speak truly, for the reasons we have stated. That the difference in respect of the swellings of the veins and of the tensive condition is not one of plethora simply, but of the more and the less within it, is clear from the following.

No part feels pain while it is being filled unless a violent stretching (τάσις) has first come about in it; [569] but if it should be raised into a swelling, yet not yet violently, it is not yet stretched. Therefore, of swellings, the one accompanied by stretching will indicate a greater plethora, and the one without it a lesser. How, then, is it that sometimes no swelling at all appears in the veins at the outset, and yet the tensive sensation is strong? For surely the condition of being stretched ought to be yoked to the very great swellings. Either it is because the swelling sometimes distends only the veins that lie in the depth; or else, if within plethora taken in relation to something, about which we are now discoursing, there is both the plethora in relation to the width of the vessels, which we call plethora, while they are not yet stretched, and the plethora in relation to the stretching of the coat, then clearly the generation of the swelling of the veins advances (ἐπιδίδοται) as the blood increases to a plethora beyond the natural due proportion of each, so that 'much' is said in relation to that proportion; whereas the stretching of the coat indicates an excess beyond the due proportion relative to the coat itself. For it is not natural for this, either, to be stretched. Each, then, is 'much': both the blood taken in relation to the natural due proportion, and the blood taken in relation to the stretching of the coat.

Erasistratus mentioned both, [570] not in an articulated way, it is true, nor as clearly as I do now, but nevertheless so as to make plain that the nature of the matter is twofold. For in saying: 'At the beginning, then, when the vessels are filled moderately, they appear more vigorous and stronger than themselves, beyond what is customary', he indicated the disproportion of the blood in excess of what is natural for each person; and in what he adds next, saying: 'but when they come further into filling, the arms and hands and shins are filled up as well', he indicated the disproportion relative to the coats that contain the blood. So there are two limits of the increase of the blood beyond what is natural: one in which the coats of the veins are filled, rising into a swelling beyond what is natural for each, and the other in which, in addition to this, it happens that they are stretched; neither of these is seen in the plethora relative to the strength. About these matters, then, this too is sufficient. Redness, which they also mention, is a sign not of plethora simply, but of sanguine plethora.

But this too will require the same qualifying distinctions as the swelling does. [571] For if it is owing to one of the external causes, such as sun, or a bath, or exercise, or walking, or, to put it simply, heating, and likewise anger, shame and all such things, then acute fevers too belong to this class. When, therefore, the condition of the whole body is uniform, and none of the things I have mentioned is present, then the redness would be a sign of a sanguineous abundance throughout the whole animal; if not, then at any rate of an abundance in that part in which it appears. For inflammations too, whether they arise in the muscles or in the skin, are attended by such a colour, since they are plethoric diseases. But concerning inflammations enough has been said in another treatise, in which we examined the swellings contrary to nature, showing that they all arise from an abundance of fluids settling down now upon one part, now upon another. Now, however, the discussion is not about these but, as was said before, about that abundance which is called plethora, when an excess of humours arises in the whole body.

But we do not say that abundance arises in the whole body in such a way that both kinds of bodies are harmed, that of the vessels and that of the fleshes. For it is possible that sometimes only one of the two is affected, so that whichever of the two parts is seized, this has occurred not in some one or two parts but either throughout the whole animal or in the most numerous and most principal parts. And accordingly, to discover of what sort the swelling (ὄγκος) is also requires a man sufficiently trained in diagnoses. In the fleshy kind, at any rate, one swelling is that of the fleshes themselves, another that of the fluids, when the flesh, like a piece of wool or a sponge, has been filled with superfluous moisture. But this kind of abundance in the fleshes is analogous to what is called, in the case of the vessels, abundance with respect to the infused content (enchyma), while the other abundance is analogous to that relative to the faculty (δύναμις), or accompanied by heaviness. We must remember that it makes no difference whether one speaks of composite flesh or of muscles, and that whenever the discussion is about the abundance in the fleshes, one must understand the muscles, not that simple flesh which is named parenchyma by some.

In the arteries and veins, however, [573] the plethora relative to the strength is not perceptible in the same way to the patients themselves; rather, only to those who are by nature most sensitive does a faint and deep-seated heaviness appear in the body. Therefore one must seek certain other, clearer signs of such a plethora. But since most physicians have been negligent about it, some not having examined it at all and others only deficiently, no surer sign has been found than the motion of the arteries, which we have expounded sufficiently in the treatises on the pulses. For the most part the veins come into a state of plethora together with the arteries, on account of the confluence of the vessels, which we have often demonstrated in other works; but sometimes, when viscous or thick humours have collected in the veins, their transfer into the arteries does not take place readily. Such a thing, however, is rare; for unless the humours are extremely thick or viscous, they will certainly flow across.

In such conditions, then, it is not possible to obtain any clear sign of the plenitude collected in the veins from the movement of the arteries, however much this may seem to be so to Nicarchus and Praxagoras, although they do not give the arteries [574] a share of blood. In the other conditions of plethora, however, one must trust the signs from the pulses, which have been stated in the treatise proper to them. The kinds of plenitude, at least when it is evenly extended into the whole body, one must distinguish as follows. The plenitude of blood is deep red; that of yellow bile is somewhat pale-yellow; it turns towards what is whiter than the natural state when phlegm prevails, just as it turns towards what is darker if black bile prevails. In each of the cases mentioned the blood too must have increased along with it. For if ever the bile called pale-yellow and yellow should be in excess by itself alone, as in the jaundiced, such an affection is no longer plenitude, nor a plethoric condition, but cacochymia. The same holds for black bile and for phlegm. But when, as was said before, there is either heaviness or bulk beyond the natural state, such a condition is called plethoric, and one must recognise from the colour the kind of the prevailing humour.

But bile alone can produce neither of the symptoms that are inseparable from plethora [575], neither the bulk nor the heaviness; for some other affection will be produced by it before it has increased to so great an extent. Phlegm alone, if indeed any humour, and not all phlegm without qualification, but that which occurs in the dropsies called leukophlegmatiai, will be able to be in excess throughout the whole body. It is clear that the so-called raw humour too must, at least in the present discussion, be counted as one of the kinds of phlegm; for if we shall posit it as different from that, then in addition to the differences of plethora we have just stated it is necessary to add also the one arising from such a humour. This humour is thicker than the other phlegm and less pneumatic, such as settles in urines, especially those which, as a result of gluttony, have a copious sediment resembling bean-pottage. Moreover, such a humour has often passed downwards all at once in those bodies that abstained from exercises but made use of very many foods, and of baths after meals. But with this humour too, as with phlegm, a certain white discoloration is present together with it throughout the whole body.

Of the other kinds of phlegm, one [576] is sweet, another sour, another salty. People become sleepy with the sweet, hungry when the sour is in excess, just as they become thirsty when the salty predominates; and they are without appetite with the raw humour mentioned before. As for sleep, with the other phlegms mentioned before it is a little more than accords with nature; but the raw humour, like the sweet phlegm, plainly makes people sleepy. For it has been shown elsewhere that when the sensory principle is moistened and cooled, the comatose condition follows, just as sleeplessness does when it is dried and heated. For this reason also those who suffer from bile are all sleepless, with either bile; but peculiar to the black bile there is present, besides, sullenness and despondency without reason. If the humours mentioned before are not in excess throughout the whole body but are collected in some one part, they produce swellings contrary to nature in the bodies themselves, about which it is shown elsewhere.

And these very symptoms of theirs just now stated, except for the loss of colour, belong to [humours] that have taken possession of the brain and the stomach [577]; for sleeplessness and sleep come about on account of the brain, and appetites and want of appetite on account of the stomach, as it is disposed now in one way, now in another. It is clear that by 'stomach' (stomachos) is now meant the mouth of the belly (gastēr), in which the phlegm that has collected, as was said a little before, produced the appetites. Of the bilious, those with yellow bile will be thirsty and nauseated, and their mouth is bitter; those with black bile are despondent, sullen, fearful, free of thirst and full of saliva; not all of them are averse to food, but some of them are. Those in whom the black [bile] has the sour quality predominating are considerably hungry; and this comes about when it is rendered more malignant. But so long as it is only like a sediment of blood, and not yet strictly sour, it is perhaps better (until it is called melancholic humour) not yet to call such a humour black bile at all, but, as I am accustomed, melancholic, because it has come close to becoming black bile.

But this is not the time to go through the differences among the cacochymias, since I said that they are not even called plenitude. Our proposed task was not simply to find out whatever is in excess in any way whatsoever, but to examine plenitude [578]; and this is an excess of the humours throughout the whole body of the animal. So in this discourse one must not long to hear the kinds either of swellings in particular parts or of cacochymia, but only of the case when either all the humours have increased in their original proportion, or one of them has acquired some slight preponderance. Now blood can acquire a very great preponderance in plethoric conditions, but none of the other humours can; for such a thing is by then called cacochymia, and no longer plenitude or plethora.

For this reason the pulses too, in cacochymias, are precisely proper to the nature of the humours; but in the plethoras mentioned they do not preserve their differences equally clearly, because the humour that is in excess is in every case together with abundant blood. But when it prevails strongly, with yellow bile the pulses must necessarily become such as we said follow when the heart is dried and heated; with black bile, in turn, such as we stated arise if it should be cooled and dried; and by the same [579] reasoning, if phlegm should ever overcome the others, it will produce pulses that are the offspring of a cold and moist condition. With blood that is exactly in accordance with nature no alteration of the original state follows; but when blood that is moister is in excess, the pulses too are altered along with it, just as if it should become hotter or colder than itself. All such matters have been distinguished in the treatise on the pulses; for now it will suffice to say this much: that from idleness and a moist regimen the blood would become moister than itself, through an excess of the watery residues; hotter, upon anger and exercises, exposures to burning heat and rubbings, a heating drug, food of that kind, and wines less diluted and older; just as, again, colder through some recent chilling. And if someone should make rather extensive use of foods that are drier in their mixture, but that have no other dyscrasia, that blood would become drier.

And indeed, in conjugation, the blood will be rendered moister and colder, or colder and drier, hotter and moister, or hotter and drier, as a result of the aforementioned [580] causes, without any of the other humours having come to predominate. But if it should also arrive at a dyscrasia through the mixture of those humours, such a dyscrasia would be constituted together with cacochymia. The blood is still said, even now, to have become either hotter, or colder and moister, and so likewise in the case of the other six dyscrasias, for there were eight in all; but this is meant in a different way, not as when the blood alone, by itself, was of such a kind.

The pulses in the eight dyscrasias will have that form which we set out in the treatise on pulses. Whether, as has been said, it belongs to the blood alone, or arises from some admixture of a humour, one must determine by the accompanying colour of the whole body and by the other symptoms (those concerning sleep and waking, or appetite and lack of appetite, or anything of that kind, which were stated a little earlier), and by the preceding regimen, and the exercises, and the things that are accustomed to befall the patient himself, and further by the season and the country and the natural density and rarity of the body. For it is better to take the assurance for the diagnosis from all of these, not from one or two, knowing well that this alone in the [581] art has the largest share in conjecture: I mean this whole diagnostic part of the art, not only that which concerns cacochymia or plethora, which we now propose to distinguish. For matters concerning the functions, or the causes of diseases, or the cures, admit of a more scientific knowledge. More has been said about these very matters elsewhere, and for now it will suffice, once we have adequately determined what has been added, to bring the writing to a close somewhere about here. The account would become adequate if it were examined by way of an example. Let it be, then, that the man is without fever, but that his veins are of greater bulk and his whole body redder.

One must therefore consider whether any of the heating causes has come near him; for if one should appear to have done so, it is better to postpone the diagnosis until the motion arising from it has settled down in the whole body, since it is not proper to bring to diagnosis someone who is angry, or has bathed, or is bathing, or has exercised, or has just taken wine, or has been heated in any other way whatsoever, but rather one who is at rest from all external motions. For if at that [582] time he should appear such, blood is in excess in the person. From there one should examine the other signs, first those that have the greatest force, then the rest in order. It was shown that these are heaviness and tension, and reluctance towards movements, and then next the features of the pulses, sleeplessness and sleep, appetites and lack of appetite, and whatever other things are of this kind. After these, each of the antecedent factors that produce plethora: whether some habitual excretion has been suppressed, whether exercise has been neglected, whether larger quantities of highly nourishing foods have been taken continually, whether he makes use of unaccustomed baths after food, and in addition to these, whether such a person is frequently seized by plethoric diseases.

On top of all these, one adds also the indications from the region and the season, or anything else of this kind, without assigning equal importance to all of them, just as one does not in the other parts of the art either. For some of the signs are scientific, such as the tension, the heaviness, the swelling of the veins, the reluctance [to move], the colour, and the movement of the pulses, provided, obviously, that all recent motions have been excluded. Others fall short of these, such as the retention of the excretions, [583] the idle life, foods that are more abundant and nourishing, and baths after food; yet all of them together come close to the scientific ones. Third in rank after these is whether the person is habitually seized by plethoric diseases. Next come the things belonging to regions and seasons that contribute to the formation of all of them. For in winter and spring, and in cold and temperate regions, people accumulate plethora more; in hot and dry seasons and regions, less. So too those who are dense at the surface accumulate it more, and those who are rarefied more rarely.
